Executive artistic director Dusty Brown tackles these themes with nuance and care. Anne Sheridan Smith, who plays Jessie Cates, the divorced, hopeless daughter of Thelma Cates, does an excellent job with the portrayal of someone who’s seemingly lost control yet still clings to it. She and Kathy Ruhl, who captures the essence of a mother who holds family secrets close to the chest yet still wants everything to work out, are a convincing, compelling duo.

For Jessie, mommy issues aren’t a trip—they’re an odyssey filled with arduous terrain, choppy waters, and endless questions. No longer interested in navigating a life with the baggage of her failures, she reveals to Thelma she’s going to use her late father’s pistol to end it all—that very night. Shockingly, she’s made a list of things for Thelma to consider and remember after she pulls the trigger, and in a dialogue filled with zingers, one that stuck with me is, “Jesus was a suicide if you ask me!,” bringing comic relief to an almost unthinkable request.

How can a mom let her kid do that? Does unconditional love include being OK with your daughter committing suicide in your home . . . with you there? How does a mother live with such grief? How does a daughter come to such conclusions, complete with meticulous instructions?

This adaptation of ʼnight, Mother is a doozy—90 minutes of breakneck revelations and gut-punching “truths.” I highly recommend this offering, but be warned—bring tissues!

What is a critic to do when a production’s many excellent parts just don’t gel? Ghostlight Ensemble Theatre Company’s The Dover Road, written by a pre-Pooh A.A. Milne, has that problem. Milne’s play, staged by Holly Robison at the Glessner House, is a satire of fussy Brits, in this case two eloping couples. The couples are convened by one Mrs. Latimer, who’s hyperfixated on ensuring that elopers are right for each other, which she ensures by locking couples in her mansion for a week at a time.

The Dover Road

Through 5/3: Thu–Sat 7:30 PM, Sun 2:30 PM; understudy performance Mon 4/27 7:30 PM; tour of Glessner House available up to one hour before showtime; Glessner House, 1800 S. Prairie, ghostlightensemble.com, pay what you can

The Dover Road, named for the Britons’ route to hop a boat to Calais, is The Drama by way of the Saw franchise, with Latimer serving as Jigsaw to the elopers. The premise also favors The Rocky Horror Show, and Maria Burnham’s Latimer has a Riff Raff in Dominic, a Scottish butler played by James Sparling. As the couples, Nick Furlong, Jean E. Mueller-Burr, Hannah Perez, and Lukas Felix Schooler are quite funny, lobbing Milne’s dialogue back and forth and selling their outsize characters. In Milne’s text, Latimer is male, and this production’s gender-bending is opaque. Perhaps it’s less unseemly for an eccentric widow to entrap unmarried women than it might be for a man, but I had trouble finding the there there.

Ghostlight’s production purports to unravel the play’s “implied observations” about gender and sexuality, but the steps it takes to, for example, bring the grooms closer would benefit from more radical textual revision. The Glessner House is a stunning backdrop (be sure to take the preshow tour!), but the tiled walls of the coach house, where the play is staged, are extremely reverberant, so the dialogue is hard to follow. Kasey Wolfgang’s costumes are a highlight, mixing knitwear and formal pieces, shedding light on Milne’s characters as soon as they appear onstage. The Dover Road is ultimately about the gaps between idealized affairs and the realities of coupling, and it’s too bad that the production has a similar tension between its parts and its whole.

A display at the Teachers for Justice curriculum fair on March 14, 2026 Credit: Lindsay Eanet

In fall 2001, weeks after the September 11 attacks, Teachers for Social Justice held their first curriculum fair, themed around what it meant to teach for justice in that tense, heavy national moment.

On March 14, almost 25 years after that first fair, and as the U.S. is engaged in more destructive and dubious wars in the Middle East, around 700 educators packed Little Village’s Social Justice High School’s auditorium for Teachers for Social Justice’s 19th Curriculum Fair, a day of workshops, speakers, and curriculum displays intended to build community, share resources, and “deepen the solidarity and political understanding essential to confront the multiple crises we face.”

“The role of schooling in the U.S. historically has not necessarily been aligned with justice frameworks and affirming life, or uplifting those that live in the margins,” said Jenine Wehbeh, a member of Teachers for Social Justice and Education Workers for Palestine, who copresented the event. “The role of education in schools right now in this moment is to allow space for young people to think and engage critically with the world around them, to center their voice and experiences, and offer points of entry into thinking about how their stories connect to the stories of people who they might not get to meet every day.”

At a time of fearmongering and national attacks on culturally responsive teaching, accurate history, and diversity, equity, and inclusion, local groups like Teachers for Social Justice and the parents of the Sustainable Community Schools initiative are organizing to educate students and each other in ways that center justice, equity, and solidarity.

Recent galvanizing moments, such as the wave of uprisings for Black liberation following the murders of George Floyd and Breonna Taylor in the summer of 2020, led to some incremental progress, Wehbeh said. And now, amid the broader backlash to diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives, organizers fear much of that progress is being rolled back. Yet the curriculum fair offers the community an opportunity to envision another future.

“This is one of those moments where we get to build that together,” she said. “Hopefully, it ripples out from here in many communities. We had over seven hundred people register today. Imagine all those pebbles in ponds rippling out. It makes a huge shift in our world.”

Teachers for Justice held its first curriculum fair in 2001. Credit: Lindsay Eanet

J. Cyriac Mathew, a social studies teacher in Back of the Yards who has been active with Teachers for Social Justice for more than 20 years, said members of his school community—students, families, teachers, and neighbors—are all experiencing different but interconnected attacks, and meeting the moment looks like using his classroom as a space where students can share their experiences.

Events like the fair are critical as spaces for the community to fight the feelings of isolation and powerlessness that can come from the headlines and strategize to respond. The layers of protection that come from teaching in Chicago, from living in a blue state, to a strong administration at his school, make opportunities like the fair all the more critical, Mathew said.

“I have no fear about teaching a culturally relevant curriculum,” he said. “We have to take advantage of spaces like that in schools in the city of Chicago because we can not only provide inspiration in places where they have a little less freedom to do this kind of work, but we can also share ideas with them and sort of be a beacon and light because all our struggles are connected.”

As a professor at the University of Illinois Chicago, Teachers for Social Justice cofounder Rico Gutstein described his circle as “a bubble in a bubble in a bubble.” He hasn’t seen the sort of anticipatory compliance around culturally responsive teaching at UIC or Chicago Public Schools (CPS) that has occurred elsewhere across the country.

“We have a moment to try and prepare ourselves and our young people to think deeply about what’s happening in the world today and make up their own minds, to think really deeply about what they’re hearing and question everything, including what they’re hearing from us,” he said. “I have the confidence in young people that they’re capable of making sense of what’s going on and doing what’s best for all of us, because that is what history has shown.”

A space for parent empowerment

Prior to her involvement with Sustainable Community Schools, Sabrina Williams, parent of a recent CPS grad, said she was focused on ensuring her child checked all the boxes of what made a “good kid” in CPS: passing tests, attending classes, and understanding the curriculum—and that had been her own educational experience as well.

“I’ve always been classified as that ‘good kid’ who never asked questions, was always following orders, following the status quo,” Williams said. “Now, I’m able to ask those lingering questions and get those questions answered in spaces where people are not only knowledgeable, but prepared to help you to move forward, and to help other parents with those same questions when it comes to being advocates for our students and our children’s rights.”

Organizers address the crowd of attendees at the Teachers for Justice curriculum fair on March 14, 2026. Credit: Lindsay Eanet

Outside of Sustainable Community Schools, Williams said she doesn’t have a space where she feels comfortable discussing political education and advocacy with other parents and community members. Having a transparent space for the community to come together empowers everyone. “Sometimes it’s uncomfortable,” she said. “A lot of these parents aren’t ready for these conversations with their kids. When they get a chance to be in those spaces, they realize they were always ready; they just didn’t get a chance to have that space to speak out about it. Now that they can, we get a lot more activated parents and community members.”

The first of the six pillars of the Sustainable Community Schools program is culturally relevant education. As her involvement has grown, Williams said she is excited about letting students know not just about their histories, but those of their classmates, communities, country, and world. “It’s something that I wasn’t awarded or given space for when I was a child, and I’m very grateful that I can do and help with it now,” she said.

Thinking globally, acting locally

The fair’s theme for 2026, “Fighting for Our Futures: Teaching for Solidarity and Justice in This Crisis,” was chosen to reflect contemporary challenges, from bombings abroad to raids by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) at home, to the ways these local and international struggles are connected, and the opportunities to effect change.

“One of the important things for us right now is the broader the attack of the MAGA agenda, the more people are swept into political consciousness,” Gutstein said. “In Minneapolis, you see people who have not been historically involved—white women from the suburbs, middle-class people coming in with the whistles around their necks—becoming engaged because their neighbors are being taken away by ICE and they feel the brunt of these injustices.”

Even as the landscape of education has evolved and challenges have changed, one constant for Teachers for Social Justice has been an emphasis on drawing connections across borders. Keynote speaker Dima Khalidi, founder and executive director of Palestine Legal, discussed efforts to repress education and discussion of Palestine, highlighting a 600 percent increase in requests for legal support from her organization. Khalidi said the crackdown is a response to the power of mobilization, particularly student-led mobilizations like walkouts and encampments. At the end of the address, a panel of students asked Khalidi what they could do as eighth graders to galvanize change. She advised them to consider different ways to learn and teach, including school clubs and reading groups.

The theme of the 2026 curriculum fair was “Fighting for Our Futures: Teaching for Solidarity and Justice in This Crisis.” Credit: Lindsay Eanet

For Williams, that bridging of international and local issues has empowered her and her community to make connections, find mutual understanding, and even space to grieve. “We talk about ICE, we talk about police brutality and how they relate to each other,” she said. “We talk about displacement, when it comes to people leaving different countries and becoming refugees, as well as displacement and public housing in Chicago. We are connected even though we don’t know that we have that connection together.”

Throughout its existence, as Teachers for Social Justice has maintained an internationalist focus, the group has also organized around local education justice issues, from fighting school closings and charter school proliferation to advocating for the Sustainable Community Schools initiative, now at 36 schools and growing, and an elected school board.

For Gutstein, maintaining and expanding on those past and present wins remains an important goal. “Having critical and culturally relevant education, the Illinois state standards give lip service to these things,” he said. “We want to fight to have the district make these things real and practiced. That’s the necessity of a strong movement to do that because it won’t happen from a proclamation. We have to fight for this.”

That history was on display at the keynote program, where Patricia Buenrostro, an educator who was part of an historic 19-day hunger strike for a neighborhood high school in Little Village, recalled young children marching down her block chanting, “Where’s our high school?” The success of that movement 25 years ago reverberated through the auditorium of the campus it helped create, as Social Justice High School principal Tinaya York greeted attendees.

“Where we at?” she asked.

“Little Village!” the crowd answered with enthusiasm.

Sharing histories, imagining futures

After the keynote, educators filed into the corridor where tables were full of art, resources, and snacks as the air buzzed with conversation and upbeat music. For Asif Wilson, a member of the Teachers for Social Justice leadership core, that burst of energy after the keynote is a highlight of the day.

“When teachers go at this work alone, when they go at it ill-resourced, when they go at it without the truths they may not recognize or know, then they are missing part of the importance of this work,” he said. “We hope that events like this and organizations like Teachers for Social Justice give teachers important homes so they can build relationships and get the resources necessary to take into their classrooms.”

An educator shows off their display at the Teachers for Justice curriculum fair on March 14, 2026. Credit: Lindsay Eanet

Many of the curricula on display focused on the connection between the global and the local such as in the collaboration “Our Struggle Is One” presented by Telpochcalli and Faraday Elementary Schools, where students made zines about the First Amendment and drew parallels between police brutality, ICE enforcement, and Gaza.

In Cristina Lara’s neuropsychylogy class, high school seniors learned about healthcare, beginning with a comparative study of healthcare systems in the U.S. and Cuba, and the impact of U.S. sanctions on the Cuban healthcare system; the unit ended with students designing their own healthcare system with a specific stakeholder in mind, whether a single parent or a pharmaceutical executive. Lara was struck by how a student described Cuba and the impact of American policy on the country as being “hidden” from her and her peers.

“Politics is entangled in every single facet of our life,” Lara said. “To try to sanitize education so that we’re not actually presenting the whole truth puts our students at a disadvantage. Once they go out in the real world, they have a right to know why things are the way they are.”

Many of the curricula covered different subjects and content areas. Host Social Justice High School showcased their sophomore capstone project, the Museum of Consumer Culture, studying the material economy. In chemistry, they learned about the extraction of resources and the impact of carbon dioxide on our atmosphere. In civics, they learned about production and labor laws in different parts of the world and analyzed advertising. To conclude, students picked one product they used and analyzed the impact of their own consumption, and presented their findings and ideas for more sustainable practices to the community and their peers.

“It’s important for us to treat students as experts and agents of change in terms of solutions,” said Social Justice High School teacher Hector Sanchez.

Lilly Cruz, founder of the El Grito and Areito Project, and Isela Ponce from Lincoln Park High School showcased student work and curricula from their unit on the history of the direct action group, the Young Lords Organization, founded by Puerto Rican youth in Chicago. What began with Cruz teaching her daughters about Puerto Rican studies at home in 2020 evolved into a curriculum cocreated with educators, students, families, and members of the Young Lords themselves. “It’s about young people learning about this story, but also understanding themselves, too,” Cruz said. “It’s asking them, ‘Who do I want to be at this moment? How do I do that with my classmates or do that in the communities I am in as I do this learning?’”

A display titled “Our Struggle Is One,” presented by Telpochcalli and Faraday Elementary Schools Credit: Lindsay Eanet

The curriculum is interdisciplinary, with an emphasis on first-person narratives, discussion, and creation of art, music, and zines. “As a Boricua, you don’t have access to yourself if you don’t have access to your stories,” Cruz said. “These are some of the most demonized stories because they talk about liberation. I think telling the truth is important, while also letting young people come to their own conclusions. There is no quote-unquote ‘indoctrinating.’ When you share the truth and share what it’s about, young people are brilliant enough to draw their own conclusions.”

In addition to the curriculum table, Cruz was among the breakout workshop presenters for the day. She planned the workshop to share several pieces from the curriculum, open a conversation about migration and the social and political contexts that created the Young Lords, and invite attendees to journal about their migration stories. These stories would become a springboard for the culminating project in the curriculum, which focuses on creating counternarratives.

“We have to be able to tell the stories that may make some people uncomfortable,” she said. “But then I get to meet a young person that says to themselves ‘Oh my gosh, they were 14? They were 16? And they were organizing for their community? They had health centers?’ These are all beautiful things, but I think it does require working with your people to build a coalition and an understanding of that.”

So far, the project has fostered unity and conversation among educators, students, and parents, Cruz said. “As we went through this process, we also realized that the parents were right there with their children, being like, ‘I knew some of this, but this is amazing and I get to share this with my young person.’”

The Mummy, in its various iterations, is a story about colonial occupation and expropriation, and the dead revenge of those who have been dispossessed. Even the truly terrible 2017 Tom Cruise version got that right. If you don’t want to tell a story about colonialism and revenge, you should not make a movie that is called The Mummy.

Director Lee Cronin clearly did not want to address those themes, but he went ahead and made a film called The Mummy anyway. It is, predictably, a mess. Endless exposition is required to get the blandly adorable middle-American Cannon family from Cairo to Albuquerque even before we start learning how Cronin has smuggled mummies into his mediocre Exorcist (1973) remake. And why are we treated to some sort of weird made-for-TV movie about candy-toting stranger danger as part of that, exactly?

The endless plot complications and the ins and outs of child possession and exodus are too tedious to detail. Even more irritating, perhaps, is the way the film drops buckets of slime and gore all over the screen in an effort to cover the lack of theme or emotional resonance. But the real problem is one of guilt.

Mummy films are fun because they always acknowledge, even if only sideways, that the putative protagonists are in fact desecraters and thieves who kind of, sort of, deserve their ancient curse. The Cannon family, though, is as devoid of sin as of personality; you’d think the ancient evil would disappear in a mighty puff of boredom as soon as it caught a whiff of them. As it is, you can’t help feeling sorry for it, trapped with us in this dry tomb of a genre exercise. No doubt it’s praying it doesn’t have to rise again for a sequel. R, 134 min.

Documentary film reflects the world—its strangest corners and its most pressing issues. At this year’s Doc10 Film Festival, falling at a time when humanity feels overwhelmed with a tempest of sociopolitical issues, the question is: What happens after we’re exposed to the problem?

“When you have a really great story that engages people,” says Doc10 cofounder Paula Froehle, “and it happens to be about a social issue, a documentary can be like rocket fuel in terms of getting people [motivated] immediately when the film ends. The first question is, what can we do?”

Entering its second decade, Doc10 is positioning itself as a robust platform for conversation and response. The 11th edition of the festival, curated by parent organization Chicago Media Project, runs from April 24 through May 3 at the Davis Theater and the Siskel Film Center. While the core of the fest remains a ten-film lineup, Doc10 is broadening its scope with the inaugural Speak Truth program, featuring seven films alongside a full program of panelists and a platform for open dialogue. This highlights Doc10’s commitment to showcasing documentary filmmaking as an active forum for engaging with the important subjects these works bring forward.

Doc10 Film Festival

Fri 4/24–Sun 5/3, Davis Theater, Siskel Film Center

Doc10’s main slate is unified by a focus on “perseverance,” according to senior programmer Anthony Kaufman, which operates less as a rigid mandate and more as a connective tissue across disparate stories. This is perhaps most telling in the programmers’ choice to place Give Me the Ball! (2026) and Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie (2026) as the festival’s first and last films, respectively.

Give Me the Ball!, directed by Liz Garbus and Elizabeth Wolff, tells the story of tennis legend Billie Jean King’s fight for gender equity and personal autonomy. It kicks off the festival with an accessible, energizing entry point, using the framework of a sports documentary to explore identity. Alex Gibney’s Knife, a film about the assassination attempt on Salman Rushdie, closes the festival with a more reflective, weighty meditation on free expression, violence, and artistic resilience. Taken together, the films frame a festival committed to resisting injustice in all its forms.

Still from Give Me the Ball! (2026)

Credit: Ellen Griesedieck/courtesy Sundance Institute

“I came up with this idea of perseverance,” Kaufman says. “It’s something that we all need right now. It’s not downbeat, right? We can fight against these things that are happening in the world.”

The theme takes many forms throughout the fest. One standout example is director Alysa Nahmias’s Cookie Queens (2026), which shows the realities of the $800 million American Girl Scout Cookies industry. It’s one of the festival’s more lighthearted entries, demonstrating how a filmmaker can balance the joys of childhood with the realities and pressures of American commerce. Meanwhile, other films explore perseverance in darker registers. Polish director Michal Marczak’s Closure (2026) follows a father who, despite every sign of hopelessness, refuses to stop searching for his son who went missing. Both films, however, reflect Kaufman’s optimism that even in difficult or uncertain times, people still push forward.

Still from Closure (2026)

Credit: Michał Marczak/courtesy Sundance Institute

The rest of the main program includes Chilean director Maite Alberdi’s A Child of My Own (2026), a story about a woman who faked her own pregnancy; filmmaker Poh Si Teng’s American Doctor, documenting three doctors working the frontlines in Gaza; Scotland-based Felipe Bustos Sierra’s Everybody to Kenmure Street (2026), telling the story of two Muslim immigrants arrested in Glasgow; Paralyzed by Hope: The Maria Bamford Story (2026), an intimate portrait of the titular comedian directed by Judd Apatow and Neil Berkeley; Remake (2026), where American documentarian Ross McElwee confronts the death of his son; and J.M. Harper’s Soul Patrol (2026), an up close look at the first Black special operations unit during the Vietnam war.

Doc10’s main slate delivers plenty of soul-stirring and poignant films, but the Speak Truth program extends an arm of direct civic engagement. The program was developed in response to institutional pressures and political urgency, with many of the selected films tied to issues like elections, free speech, environmental disaster, and immigration. Some highlights include Steal This Story, Please! (2025), in which Carl Deal and Tia Lessin trace the life of journalist Amy Goodman to underscore the importance of independent journalism, and The Librarians (2025), directed by Kim A. Snyder, which explores book banning in Texas and Florida. Crucially, these screenings are structured to move beyond passive reflection, and the inclusion of advocacy organizations will provide pathways for the audience to translate their emotional reactions into concrete activism.

Still from Steal This Story, Please! (2025)

Credit: courtesy Doc10

“Doc10, as a platform, raises the visibility for so many films and filmmakers, but it also provides the means for people to come together and to focus really deeply on issues that are really important,” Froehle says.

Across the board, Doc10 foregrounds the theater as a shared in-person space where meaning is shaped not just by the film, but by audiences experiencing it together.

“These are cinematic documentaries; these are films that we think are really important to show in a movie theater,” Kaufman emphasizes.

The films may end, but Doc10 insists that the responsibility doesn’t. This tight selection of films positions nonfiction cinema as a means of tapping into emotional clarity and offers a concise platter of documentary art that intends to move its audience.

“Art has this incredible power,” Froehle says, “to fight back, to raise your voice, to connect across different ways of thinking.”

Singer-songwriter Angel Abaya became Gelli Haha by flipping her own script. Born in Hawaii and raised in Boise, Idaho, she played violin and piano as a child, and by 18 she’d immersed herself in Boise’s music scene. In 2021, Abaya relocated to Los Angeles, and in 2023, under her own name, she released her first full-length album, a collection of moody, dreamy indie pop called The Bubble. But she was tired of the pressure to be seen as a “serious artist,” and she realized she’d been applying most of it herself. So she bought an all-red wardrobe and developed the alter ego of Gelli Haha, where she can use synth pop, dance, and performance art to let her freak flag fly. The Moviegoer is the diary of a local film buff, collecting the best of what Chicago’s independent and underground film scene has to offer.

I’d argue Chicago is one of the great cities for experimental film, and the Onion City Experimental Film Festival is a big reason for that. Last week’s edition was its 36th, curated this year by Elise Schierbeek and Nicky Ni. (Both previously worked for the Video Data Bank at the School of the Art Institute and were part of recent controversial layoffs.)



I liked much of what I saw; many of my friends had work in the festival, and of course I admire what they do. Of the films I saw in person—admittedly only two competition programs, due to scheduling conflicts—I was struck by Brittany Gravely’s Mist (2025), which won a juror prize; Ben Russell’s Another Earth (2025); and Sam Taffel and Gillian Waldo’s Learning from Learning from Las Vegas (2025). Haunting and ethereal, Mist documents the titular phenomenon “days after the death of a friend,” per the description. Through its grainy black-and-white cinematography, the film evokes both grief and death, the sadness of still living and the surreality of passing.

Still from Learning from Learning from Las Vegas (2025) Credit: courtesy Onion City Experimental Film Festival

In Another Earth, against a backdrop of similarly ghostly images more menacing than mournful, a voice quotes Rachel Kushner’s novel Creation Lake, referring to those who endeavor to outlive circumstances that threaten humanity, repeating over and over: “They think, ‘I’ll be the clever one, the one who survives mass death.’ But why would you want to survive mass death? What will be the purpose of life if life were reduced to a handful of armed pessimists hoarding canned food and fearing each other?” It’s not a prescient assertion, but it’s an all-too-timely one: With atrocities like the genocide in Palestine and the burgeoning war in Iran, and the existential threats posed by climate change and AI, among many others, one wonders what the hope is for the people who think they’re the exceptions to such terrible rules. Is it really living if it’s at the expense of so much human life?

Learning from Learning from Las Vegas takes as its inspiration Robert Venturi, Denise Scott Brown, and Steven Izenour’s 1972 book Learning from Las Vegas, with Taffel and Waldo as stand-ins for Venturi and Scott Brown, who were married. The filmmaking duo aren’t wed in real life—they joked during the Q&A that the biggest risk they took in making the film was their friendship—but it’s nevertheless a thought-provoking concept to embody this arcane duo vis-à-vis their book on postmodern architecture in Sin City. The bright lights and stark kitsch of Las Vegas are naturally the backdrop for this consideration; I was impressed by how controlled it felt against the sprawling desert of iniquity.

On Sunday night, as part of the Doc Films series Robert Beavers: My Hand Outstretched to the Winged Distance and Sightless Measure, the filmmaker appeared in person to introduce the screening and participate in a Q&A. His filmsFrom the Notebook of . . . (1971/1998), The Painting (1972/1999), and Dedication: Bernice Hodges (2024) played. I won’t pretend to be overly familiar with Beavers’s work (the series will help to fill this blind spot), but I thought it was interesting when he referred to watching a film in a theater as a “projection event.” To me, moviegoing is exciting, something I post about on social media or write about in my journal as if I were going to Coachella. Sometimes, though, it strikes me that, to others, what I’m doing most likely seems like just going to the movies (albeit a lot more often than the average person). But now that I can think of them as projection events, well . . .

Until next time, moviegoers.

Chicago takes its public art seriously. The murals and installations we have on view represent us, our communities, our values—from the Haymarket Memorial in the West Loop to Alexander Calder’s iconic Flamingo to Kerry James Marshall’s gorgeous mural on the side of the Chicago Cultural Center. After Casa Aztlan was whitewashed by developer City Pads in 2017, the community backlash was so quick and so strong that Ray Patlán and other artists were promptly hired to paint a new mural. When a mural by artist Gabriel Villa was commissioned on private property in Bridgeport—and then quickly graffiti blasted by the city at the request of then-alderman James Balcer—the local and national art communities widely condemned the censorship, leading to coverage from WBEZ and the Huffington Post, among other outlets.

So it should come as no surprise that a recent mural of the late Ukrainian refugee Iryna Zarutska, painted at the behest of Ireland-born, Bay Area–based tech entrepreneur Eoghan McCabe, has received a fair amount of scrutiny. Completed in January, the mural is located at 2415 W. Montrose, in North Center. It’s part of a nationwide effort spearheaded by McCabe called Remember Iryna, which is funding similar murals across the country.

The 23-year-old Zarutska, who had emigrated to the U.S. in 2022, was killed in August 2025 during a random attack on a light-rail in North Carolina. She had no ties to Chicago. McCabe, 42, is one of the founders of an AI-powered help-desk platform called Intercom. Like other young tech founders, he has a tendency to shitpost on social media. (Sample tweets include: “It is the duty of men to protect society, to kill the monsters and create a world where all good people can be well,” and “It feels like almost every day now a violent crime on the tiny island of Ireland occurs where ‘the suspect’s nationality is not allowed to be made public.’ Everyone knows what that means.”)

He posted frequently about Zarutska’s tragic death after surveillance video of her attack was released, and it became a rallying point for the far-right to condemn the criminal justice system. (Her attacker, DeCarlos Brown Jr., had a history of prior arrests.) McCabe put out a call on X, asking for donations to fund a series of murals of Zarutska, which led to a $1 million pledge from Elon Musk. The murals started appearing late last year, in cities like New York and Miami, and then in Chicago.

Community response was quick and veered negative. In March, the North Center mural was vandalized—and it wasn’t the first time. It’s not unheard of for murals in our city to memorialize the dead—but those tributes are usually requested by locals, and painted by them, too. (Zarutska’s mural was painted by SAV45, an artist based in Spain.)

What distinguishes the murals that Chicago holds most dear is the process that made them—one rooted in community engagement. Remember Iryna is totally devoid of community involvement and thus worth examining further. Should we even consider such a project public art?

Chicago’s abundance of murals can be traced back to the Wall of Respect, the now-iconic 1967 mural that honored heroes of the Black community—people whose importance, according to historian Rebecca Zorach, “was undervalued by mainstream white culture.”

Located on the side of a corner store at 43rd Street and Langley Avenue in Bronzeville, the Wall of Respect was the work of a group of Black American artists from the Organization for Black American Culture (OBAC, pronounced o-ba-see). It featured more than 50 notable Black figures, from Malcolm X to Muhammad Ali to Gwendolyn Brooks. “A mural about the black American experience was not exactly a novelty,” former Reader writer Jeff Huebner wrote, in one of several articles on the artists and the mural movement they spawned. But the “Wall of Respect was the first outdoor mural done for the community—for everyone.”

The Wall of Respect helped spur the community mural movement.

Courtesy Georg Stahl Mural Collection/University of Chicago Library

Its community engagement was done on the fly. William Walker, one of the mural artists, secured permission from the business owner and spoke with local community members to gain approval. And while surely not every person living near the corner at the time supported the Wall of Respect, it’s clear that plenty of people took pride in it. Local kids offered tours of it; neighborhood street gangs kept a watchful eye on it. In Zorach’s book, Art for People’s Sake: Artists and Community in Black Chicago, 1965–1975, she recounts a recollection from artist Jeff Donaldson, “People feel better when they walk by there, and we made it so.”

“The Wall of Respect was a sort of early kind of experiment in that respect, where the methods and practices [of community engagement] hadn’t been fully developed,” said Zorach, who coauthored a book on the mural with Abdul Alkalimat and Romi Crawford. Zorach notes that the nature of mural painting easily lends itself to a collaborative process between artists and passersby. “Very often, just because of the way that it has to be done—with artists working outside on the street and people walking by—there’s going to be conversation, and there’s going to be questions, and there’s a sort of communication and collaboration that develops out of that.”

The Wall of Respect’s impact was fast and powerful. In 1968, Huebner writes, a similar mural was commissioned in Detroit, and Black pride murals followed in Boston, Saint Louis, and Philadelphia. The community mural movement, as it became known, laid the groundwork for much public art that exists today: art that tells community history, depicts important cultural figures, or portrays an uplifting narrative about a people or neighborhood. Community buy-in was a crucial component of that, whether that meant a local group commissioned a work, its subject matter was publicly discussed or voted on, or community members otherwise had some opportunity to share their desires for a work.

Janice Bond, the executive director of the Chicago Public Art Group, explained that many of her organization’s projects seek to engage the community, which could mean people who live around the proposed site or a demographic that the artwork intends to represent. “We are creating art with community, not for community,” Bond said. “Community engagement varies from project to project in different degrees. The important part for us is that it happens, and that there is at least some sort of opportunity for the community to be heard, especially if it is content of a sensitive nature.”

“A lot of times I’ve walked away from projects if there isn’t a community buy-in.”

Sam Kirk

Sam Kirk is a Little Village–based artist whose artwork can be found throughout the city. They painted La Villita Skate Park; spearheaded Las Puertas de Paseo Boricua in Humboldt Park; helped create The Love That I Vibrate, on the side of Howard Brown Health Center in Northalsted; and the I Am Logan Square mural at Kedzie and Milwaukee, among many other projects.

The level of community engagement depends on the project—whether it’s a public or private commission, and on the subject matter. But most of Kirk’s work focuses on social justice issues, “so community buy-in is extremely important.”

“Usually when the conversation happens, we’re not really talking about the design of the mural. Kirk points to their 2021 mural, Stronger Together, led by the Little Village organization New Life Centers, which sought to ease racial tension in the neighborhood following the murder of George Floyd and the subsequent uprisings, as a perfect example of a community-led project. “The mural was a part of a larger community project that’s still actually running, to unite north and south Lawndale,” Kirk said. “There were workshops and healing circles, and different community engagement programs, like just basketball, to bring youth from Little Village and North Lawndale together, to do fun things, to build upon joy together.”

The larger issue was that Brown had a diagnosis of schizophrenia, which was often untreated as his family struggled to secure him long-term care. This problem is hardly unique to Brown. According to a 2022 survey from the National Council for Mental Wellbeing, 42 percent of U.S. adults who said they needed mental health treatment in the previous 12 months didn’t receive it due to costs or other barriers. As Pew has reported, less than half of people with serious mental illness, like schizophrenia, are receiving care: “Many receive treatment only in jails or prisons, which have become the de facto institutions for people with [severe mental illness] because we no longer have sufficient public hospital beds for them.”

Trump and his proxies have painted Brown as less than human. McCabe, for his part, shared several horrific screenshots of the attack on his X account, calling Brown a “monster.”

McCabe launched his mural campaign in September, just days after the video of Zarutska’s murder was released. Murals started popping up last year—in Washington, D.C., New York, LA, and then Chicago. Some of the artists and businesses who have participated in the mural project thus far have either denied any knowledge of the founder’s political leanings or tried to argue that the work wasn’t political. Ben Keller, an artist who painted murals of Zarutska in Washington, D.C., and New York City, told the Tribune that he “tries to stay away from the political noise because it can taint the murals’ message.” In Providence, the owners of a bar where a mural was slated to appear wrote in a statement that it was “never intended to be political.” The artist involved, Ian Gaudreau, said his artwork was “meant to combat the idea of it being used for a political agenda.”

Yet it takes just a cursory glance at McCabe’s X account to ascertain his political motivations. Among tweets praising Musk and Trump are racist and xenophobic remarks like, “One of the great sorrows of my life has been watching my beautiful home country of Ireland be destroyed by its own unfettered immigration policy. As of the end of last year there were 1.2M immigrants out of a total population of 5.38M.” The Chicago Reader’s requests for comment from McCabe and Musk went unanswered.

The local Ukrainian population has also been divided on the mural. Halyna Parasiuk, an archivist at the Ukrainian National Museum of Chicago, told the Sun-Times that “it’s good to keep this memory of this innocent girl.” Ukrainian artist Aliona Solomadina, who fled Ukraine in 2022, wrote in an email to the Reader that the tragedy “has been politicized within the American context,” noting that Zarutska was not attacked for being Ukrainian or a refugee, but “simply because she was sitting near the attacker.”

“From my perspective as an artist and designer, the mural as a medium isn’t appropriate for this story, especially given this politicization,” she wrote. “There are many other ways to support Ukrainian refugees, such as providing jobs or donating to volunteer organizations.”

Mariya Dmytriv-Kapeniak, president of the Ukrainian Congress Committee of America Illinois chapter, told the Sun-Times that she is in communication with Zarutska’s community in North Carolina, and that the family had not granted permission to use Zarutska’s likeness.

Knowing the hate-filled rhetoric behind the project, it’s hard to argue that Remember Iryna is a sincere attempt at memorializing her life. Nor does it merit an earnest conversation about free speech or the value of public art. It doesn’t hold a candle to the murals in our city that were forged in a participatory manner, that seek to tell people’s histories. McCabe is a founder of a billion-dollar company, as is Musk. They have the funds to make their opinions heard in a myriad of ways; the hundreds of thousands, or even a million, they spent on this campaign have yielded dividends in terms of influence. Perhaps the best course of action for their project is to ignore it.

Workers at the American Library Association announced on March 2 that they are forming a new union, ALA Workers United. After registering with the National Labor Relations Board in early April, the nonprofit’s workers will vote on April 24 on whether to recognize it. Headquartered in Chicago, ALA advocates for libraries across the country at the federal level and helps them better serve their communities.

Founded in 1876, ALA is the largest library association in the world, with satellite offices in Washington, D.C., and Middletown, Connecticut, in addition to its Chicago office. The organization’s workers serve as the bridge between the 47,000 members, who include librarians, library staff, and library supporters, and the organization’s resources. Some of their most visible work includes organizing events for librarians to network, publishing books for the academic field of librarianship, lobbying Congress for support for library funding, and providing broadband internet access to underserved communities. Notably, on April 14, ALA and the American Federation of State, County & Municipal Employees (AFSCME) reached a settlement with the Department of Justice to protect the Institute of Museum and Library Services, ensuring the agency can continue to support libraries and museums across the country.

If recognized, ALA Workers United will be joining the 13 cultural institutions that have unionized in Chicago since the pandemic shutdown, walking the fiery path paved by AFSCME Council 31. In an open letter, more than 40 ALA workers state that “recent multi-round layoffs, increased workloads, benefits reductions, financial crises, ingrained salary disparities, and lack of transparent decision-making” motivated their organizing. Employees launched a petition that they hope other union members, librarians, and library supporters will sign to show their support for the new union. More than 35,000 library workers nationwide—including over three thousand in the Chicago area—are themselves unionized and represented by AFSCME.

The ALA’s operating budget comes from member dues, its yearly conference, and other revenue streams, including publishing, continuing education, and contributed support, according to ALA leadership. The organization’s conference was disrupted in 2020 and 2021.

Over the past six years, COVID social distancing and federal cuts to social service funds have strained libraries and organizations like ALA that support them. In July 2025, ALA management announced a “strategic plan” to address a growing operating deficit, but the plan’s rollout has left workers feeling vulnerable.

“[Our employer told us] another way that they were going to help with the funding [deficit] was to not contribute to our retirement,” said Katina Jones, a data analyst who works in the Public Library Association division of the nonprofit. In October 2025, ALA informed employees that their 3 percent match on employee contributions would be suspended for 2026. “That probably was the biggest red flag,” said Jones.

The amount ALA would save from cutting their retirement plan fund was, Jones said, it raised more questions than it answered. ALA also informed workers at that time that there would be no salary increases.

“This was a difficult but measured step, and we will continue to evaluate reinstating the match as financial conditions evolve,” said Dan Montgomery, ALA’s executive director, in a response to the Reader.

The union told the Reader that ALA facilitated voluntary layoffs in May 2025, followed by a round of layoffs in July and October. After October, when 8 percent of staff were laid off, Jones said other workers had to pick up their tasks. “We got rid of people, but we didn’t get rid of any deliverables.” Jones’ former coordinator was responsible for internal and external customer service tasks. But they were laid off, and now it’s Jones who processes employee invoices and replies to emails from the division’s 9,000 members, even though her position as a data analyst should not involve that work.

Colton Ursiny, who has worked in ALA’s continuing education division for a decade, is excited for the union. He believes unions are a way of bringing democracy into practice in their everyday lives, and libraries are the cornerstone of democracy. “It’s incredibly unsustainable,” Ursiny said. “We are losing staff to retirement, to people burning out, to layoffs. It’s not a good situation here, and I think that a union will help protect us. We need to foster a work culture, practices, pay, and benefits that encourage people to stay with ALA . . . and to feel motivated to do the work that they need to do.”

Ursiny said the union efforts are the staff’s best chance to bring the strategic vision to life by creating a sustainable staffing environment that allows the organization to thrive for another 150 years.

Credit: Courtesy ALA Workers United

Staff began organizing formally and meeting regularly in November 2025, but conversations about it had already begun, with the original seeds planted in the summer of 2025. To be official, the new group will need more than 50 percent of “yes” votes from union-eligible workers who vote in their April 24 election.

“I know that staff have shared concerns as part of their recent decision to organize, and I take those perspectives seriously,” said Montgomery. “The past several years have brought significant change across the ALA, including financial pressures that required difficult but necessary decisions to stabilize ALA and strengthen its position for the future. Throughout this period, our focus has remained on advancing our mission while making responsible choices to support long-term fiscal health.”

Montgomery said the nonprofit is actively realigning internal structures to support more sustainable workloads. But ALA also respects workers’ right to organize, and is committed to engaging in that process thoughtfully and in good faith.

“Despite these many challenges,” the ALA Workers United March 2 letter reads, “we still believe ALA is an inspiring place to work and want to see it succeed.”

The corporate world instills a very particular type of anxiety: Each day mirrors the last, and the future holds more of the same. This malaise-filled white-collar grind is hardly new. It’s the backbone of Gen X classics, from the violent Fight Club (1999) to the much more comedic Office Space (1999). But the feeling has only intensified, as stagnant wages and rising costs make forward movement feel out of reach. That anxiety is the only reason anyone could justify a movie based on the puzzle-box horror video game The Exit 8, which traps its player in an endlessly repeating hallway.

Director Genki Kawamura’s film adaptation is as faithful as possible to the viral Japanese video game. The game, which received more than 2 million downloads despite its shockingly simple premise, has players assume the role of a person trapped in an underground subway passage that suddenly mutates into a repeating labyrinth. The player must attempt to push forward toward the titular exit, but if they find an anomaly, they must turn back. It’s a maddeningly simple premise, but one that resonates with generations of people who might feel stuck in the same cycle every day.

Kawamura’s film sticks pretty close to the boundaries laid out by the video game, injecting the looping narrative with J-horror sensibilities. Exit 8 opens with the first-person perspective of the “Lost Man,” played by Kazunari Ninomiya. This weary protagonist spends the beginning of the movie threading through crowds of subway riders, many of whom barely look up from their phones, as he attempts to get to his temp job. All the while, his ex-girlfriend is calling to tell him she’s pregnant. Kawamura uses the first-person view to place us squarely in the Lost Man’s embattled life, right up until the moment he is stuck.

What follows is essentially a one-to-one rendering of the video game. The protagonist traverses the endlessly looping tunnels, emerging at the same place over and over again: a sterile hallway, where a man with a briefcase (Yamato Kochi) walks past him, blank-faced. The film is relatively heavy-handed, much like a video game where the rules are plastered on the side. In many cases, I’d admonish this decision, but Kawamura delivers something so sure of itself that it demands to be understood at face value. In fact, the director rarely injects additional bits of mythology to help explain the absurd purgatory. It speaks for itself.

Still, parts of the film do hint at what this maze might symbolize. The Lost Man is noticeably trepidatious about the idea of having a child. Meanwhile, the section that focuses on the man with a briefcase, known as “the Walking Man,” nods to the hell of corporate life and death by overwork (“karoshi” in Japanese). But Kawamura rarely dives into these ideas. Instead, he subjects the audience to the same repetitive cycle of the video game: Over and over, the trapped men make the same mistakes.

This premise might not always have succeeded, but it fits within a body of work that grapples with maddening endlessness. Tim Robinson’s 2025 series The Chair Company probes the meaninglessness of everything, and the upcoming film Backrooms, directed by Kane Parsons (aka Kane Pixels), draws from an Internet meme about the absurdity and liminality of office spaces. It’s trite to call it “Kafkaesque,” yet there’s no other term that fits this suffocating, cyclical nightmare that presses down on the global psyche.

Despite its message, Exit 8 is frustrating as a viewer. It’s often too reliant on jump scares and a terrifying score by Yasutaka Nakata and Shohei Amimori. These elements alone don’t allow the film to supersede its source material; it lacks the emotionality needed to care for these characters or empathize with their dilemmas. Furthermore, it fails to capture the immediate, tactical suspense one might experience in a first-person video game. This film is a game worth playing once, then shelving, perhaps forever. PG-13, 95 min.

The Merry Wives of Windsor, according to late critic Harold Bloom, gives audiences a “False Falstaff,” one far removed from both the pathos and the wit of Prince Hal’s drinking buddy in Henry IV, Part 1 and Part 2. Still, as Bloom also notes, the Falstaff of Merry Wives inspired Verdi’s eponymous opera—so his creation in Shakespeare’s comedy (circa 1597) isn’t a total bust. (Allegedly, Shakespeare wrote it at the request of Queen Elizabeth I, who wanted a play that showed Falstaff in love.)



Philip Breen’s high-spirited and low-comedy extravaganza at Chicago Shakespeare makes clear the lines between the Bard’s bawdy caper and British sex farces such as Ray Cooney’s Run for Your Wife. But as is almost always the case with Shakespearean comedies, its author was smart enough to make the women the real stars of the show.

The Merry Wives of Windsor

Through 5/3: Wed 1 and 7 PM, Thu–Fri 7 PM, Sat 2 and 7 PM, Sun 2 PM; also Thu 4/23 1 PM and Tue 4/28 7 PM; audio description Sun 4/26 2 PM, open captions Wed 4/29 1 and 7 PM, ASL interpretation Fri 5/1 7 PM; Chicago Shakespeare Theater, 800 E. Grand, 312-595-5600, chicagoshakes.com, $66-$128

The plot unfolds through a series of episodes involving Sir John Falstaff (Jason Simon), who is hanging out in Windsor doing what he usually does: drinking, gambling, and plotting seductions in order to attain the funds for the first two activities. In this case, he’s determined to have his way with two married women: Mistress Page (Ora Jones) and Mistress Ford (Issy van Randwyck), both very comfortably middle-class and (so he believes), ready to step out on their husbands and open their, er, hearts (and purses) to him. When the two women discover that Falstaff has sent them near-identical wooing letters, they plot their revenge.



That’s most of the play, though there is a thin subplot surrounding the marriage plans of the Pages’ daughter, Anne (Olivia Pryor), and a silly pseudo-duel between the preening Dr. Caius (Nate Burger), the local French dentist, and the Welsh parson, Hugh Evans (Nick Sandys, who also serves as fight coordinator)—both employing comically exaggerated accents. The former’s long-suffering receptionist, Mistress Quickly (Nancy Voigts) serves as the go-between for the wives as they plot their various humiliations upon the fat man (including the famous scene where he’s tossed into a large laundry basket).



The husbands and the other men in this story of the merry wives are entirely ancillary, though Master Ford (Timothy Edward Kane) nails the jealous sad sack who clumsily tries to set his own trap for the wife he (wrongly) suspects of infidelity. (A scene where his toupee flops down over his forehead as he weeps is both incredibly funny and painfully pathetic.) Scenic and costume designer Max Jones brings a contemporary Halloween flavor to the proceedings (suitable for a play that lives and dies by the “tricks” enacted by the title characters as well as the disguises adopted by several characters), while sound designer and composer Lindsay Jones brings in totally unsubtle (and hence perfect) song cues, such as Marvin Gaye’s “Let’s Get It On” during Mistress Ford’s first fake assignation with Falstaff.



Merry Wives is never going to be one of my favorite Shakespeare comedies: The stakes are too low to fully identify with the characters. But low stakes require precisely rendered sight gags and verbal dexterity to hold our attention, and that’s what Breen’s cast (which also includes reliable comic talents like Alex Weisman, Chiké Johnson, and Paul Oakley Stovall) offers in generous abundance.

In 2008, a woman in Ness City, Kansas, was found literally stuck to her boyfriend’s toilet seat, where she had been living for the past two years. She wasn’t imprisoned: It was apparently a choice she made that was enabled by her boyfriend, who brought her food and water every day while asking her if she would come out. Her daily response? “Maybe tomorrow.”



That strange and sad story provided the impetus for Max Mondi’s one-act, Maybe Tomorrow, now in a local premiere with Wild Door Theater under Andrew Gallant’s direction. Wild Door made their local debut in fall 2025 with a revival of Noah Haidle’s Smokefall. In that production, Isabella Isherwood played Beauty, a daughter who stopped speaking entirely and began eating paint and dirt after hearing her father complain about the noise in the house and the cost of feeding his children. So she’s no stranger to playing characters who make extreme choices in response to family upheaval.

Maybe Tomorrow

Through 5/24: Fri 7:30 PM, Sat 3 and 7:30 PM, Sun 3 PM; Athenaeum Center for Thought and Culture, 2936 N. Southport, wilddoortheater.com, $43 (students/seniors $29)

Here, Isherwood plays Gail, a struggling artist who also runs a storefront crafts shop in Vermont while living in a trailer (or deluxe mobile home, if you prefer) with her husband, Ben (Lucky Star). An unexpected pregnancy sends them to Gary, Indiana, where the aimless Ben, a sometime mechanic, finds a new job selling luxury used cars—and Gail retreats into the bathroom, or what she and Ben have dubbed “the pause room.” Only here, the pause extends into years of isolation, where Gail lives on the toilet and makes beaded jewelry for her Etsy shop to support her family, while mostly denying the existence of Benji, the son she has with Ben, who is essentially functioning as a single father.

The only people she talks to regularly, aside from perfunctory conversations with Ben (where the phrase “maybe tomorrow” does indeed get a workout) are the audience members. She asks us to look away as she changes her top covered in infant vomit (back when she was still changing her clothes, and caring for her son). She decides that she is indeed simply in a play, while telling us about how much she hates plays, like Edward Albee’s Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?, where characters are talked about but never seen. (The fact that she’s talking about the son that George and Martha in Albee’s play have invented for themselves is an early harbinger of how she’s going to deal with Benji.)

The breaking of the fourth wall feels a bit precious at points in Mondi’s play, which debuted off-Broadway last year with Abingdon Theatre Company. And the obvious mental illness underlying Gail’s condition isn’t named. You could call it postpartum depression, but the signs are there before Benji arrives. At the beginning of the play, Isherwood appears in an orange prison jumpsuit and Star arrives dressed as a guard. It soon becomes clear that this is part of their sex lives (at least until Benji is born). Mondi’s not kink-shaming, but where the kink in, say, the film Secretary (2002) becomes a way for two isolated people to connect, the prison motif plays out here with disquieting questions as to who is actually in charge. Star’s costumes (designed by Saawan Tiwari) play with the orange palette of the jumpsuit, suggesting that the tables have turned and Ben is essentially a prisoner to Gail’s defiant self-imposed isolation.

The script’s unwillingness to pathologize or offer easy explanations is both a strength and a weakness. It’s easy to imagine a less compelling actor than Isherwood wearing out their welcome as Gail, even though Mondi’s play does raise potent questions about gendered assumptions around breadwinning and caregiving. But though there are moments where the story becomes a bit self-conscious (again, mostly in Gail’s direct addresses to the audience), it’s largely an interesting and well-acted snapshot of how easily extreme choices can become normalized by the ones who love us.

After years of planning, fundraising, lobbying, and other preparations, leaders at the Chicago South Side Birth Center are closer than ever to establishing the first independent, Black midwife–led maternity care facility in the city’s majority Black south-side neighborhoods. In early April, the nonprofit’s leaders were joined by political representatives, community partners, neighbors, birth workers, funders, and other local leaders for a groundbreaking ceremony at 8301 S. South Shore in the city’s South Chicago neighborhood on the far south side.

Donning hard hats and armed with shovels, Chicago South Side Birth Center founder and lead steward Jeanine Valrie Logan was joined by Chicago mayor Brandon Johnson, Illinois lieutenant governor and Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Juliana Stratton, Tenth Ward alderperson Peter Chico, and Chicago Department of Planning and Development commissioner Ciere Boatright. Together, they and others symbolically broke ground by pouring piles of dirt at the birth center’s future location, where construction began earlier this year.

“What we’re creating here at Chicago South Side Birth Center is truly legacy, not only for ourselves but for our whole community,” said Valrie Logan. “This work we’re doing together involves actualizing the visions and dreams of those who have come before us.”

Government officials and community leaders at the groundbreaking for the Chicago South Side Birth Center on April 7, 2026. Credit: Roger Morales

Liz Dozier, founder and CEO of the philanthropic organization Chicago Beyond, which reportedly contributed $1.5 million to the Chicago South Side Birth Center’s construction costs and where Valrie Logan is employed as a leader in residence to develop the birth center, called the day “special . . . and it’s not just because we’re breaking ground. It’s because we’re standing in the middle of something that should have always existed.”

The yearslong project to establish an independent Black midwife–led birth center is expected to be completed in early 2027 and aims to bring community-based, holistic reproductive healthcare, childbirth education, pre- and postnatal care, lactation support, and community wellness programming to the south side, which has historically lacked access to comprehensive healthcare services.

Valrie Logan has worked to open the Chicago South Side Birth Center since she founded the organization in 2021. Research shows that Black midwives and doulas significantly improve outcomes in Black maternal healthcare by providing culturally appropriate care, advocacy, and emotional support, as well as mitigating the impact of medical racism, in turn reducing pregnancy-related deaths. In Illinois, Black women are twice as likely to die from pregnancy-related causes and three times as likely to die from pregnancy-related medical complications as white women, according to the Illinois Department of Public Health.

The creation of the birth center followed the passage of legislation that increased the number of birth centers allowed to operate in Illinois. The project’s completion has been delayed multiple times due to changing construction costs, zoning challenges that come with turning a church into a birth center, and the task of educating government bureaucrats about doulas when “people don’t really know what a birth center is,” Valrie Logan said. Nonetheless, she believes the state of U.S. reproductive healthcare and the politics around it have contributed to the support the Chicago South Side Birth Center has received in recent years. “I think it was a lot to do with the national landscape of the maternal health crisis and then the state really getting behind [us], . . . but I think with the government and philanthropy really being like, ‘This is something important and that we need to be putting our money into,’ I think helped move the narrative around, like, this is something that should be accessible to folks in community,” Valrie Logan said.

Last year, the Chicago South Side Birth Center received a $3.3 million community development grant from the city, part of the $8.1 million the center raised in a capital campaign that ended in June. Valrie Logan said the center received donations from individuals, foundations, philanthropists, and state and city governments. In 2023, the Chicago South Side Birth Center crowdsourced roughly one-third of the funds used to purchase its location, according to Block Club Chicago.

Valrie Logan, left, at the groundbreaking for the Chicago South Side Birth Center on April 7, 2026. Credit: Roger Morales

During the ceremony, Johnson spoke, in part, about the importance of the city providing financial support to projects like the Chicago South Side Birth Center that aim to address gaps in Chicago’s reproductive healthcare options, and wanted to see a similar birth center on the city’s west side. “The real, harsh realities of the gaps with maternal healthcare that our mothers, especially Black mothers, have experienced, they’re not new,” said Johnson. “But they are certainly the result of decades of disinvestment and neglect, and now we find ourselves in a moment when our disparities and these demands for resources, that attention, is now being granted to the very people who’ve been calling for it.”

Johnson also criticized the federal government for gutting funding to cities such as Chicago that invest in reproductive healthcare. He added that he’s looking forward to voting for Stratton in November’s general election, saying she could “take this fight to the federal government.”

During her remarks, Stratton called attention to her efforts to “champion our state’s birth equity initiative to expand access to the full spectrum of reproductive care in light of the very real Black maternal mortality crisis in this state and this nation” as well as her own experience as a mother to four daughters, including one whose birthday was that same day. “Today is not just about construction. It’s not just about shovels and dirt and blueprints. Today is about rewriting the narrative about what’s possible in maternal wellness when we center community and follow the lead of Black midwives,” Stratton said. “Just as I tell my daughters the stories of the day they were born, I can only imagine the stories that will emerge out of this building, stories of no longer having to get on two or three buses to access the reproductive care that you need and deserve because now it’s available right here on the south side.”

Several other local representatives and community leaders offered remarks, including Chico, who discussed the importance of expanding reproductive healthcare options on the south side and said Valrie Logan was a doula for his cousin during her pregnancy. The Chicago South Side Birth Center groundbreaking also included a ceremonial land blessing from the members of the Chicago American Indian Community Collaborative.

Family and friends of Valrie Logan were also in attendance at the ceremony, including Ifarinu “MamaAfrica” Egunrinde, artist and owner of Mama Africa’s Marketplace, who met Valrie Logan after surviving a difficult birth experience and developing a fear of hospitals. Valrie Logan later acted as the doula and midwife for Egunrinde’s second and third pregnancies. As the Chicago South Side Birth Center enters its next phase, Egunrinde said she feels grateful that Black and Brown south siders will have a space to receive safe, holistic reproductive healthcare. “Pregnancy and birth is already kind of scary,” she said. “Bringing in life, knowing that the smallest thing could end both lives, it’s kind of that precious balance of joy and fear and happiness [and] excitement. . . . To know that [there’s] a safe space here for our community to give birth, and to bring life and care for the mothers [and their] children and then their children and then their children and their children and their children—it’s important. We need more of them.”

While Valrie Logan feels she’s already made great progress on the birth center, she said there’s still much work to do, including securing ongoing funding, fighting for legislation to ensure birthworkers are paid fairly, and advocating for birth equity locally and nationwide. “This is a huge win for Chicago—but the work isn’t over.”

Chicago musicians and composers Dustin Laurenzi and Matt Gold have their hands in many pots. Gold is a versatile guitarist who’s lent his talents to the likes of Makaya McCraven, Jamila Woods, and Marquis Hill while releasing his own material (including a standout 2025 collaboration with Resavoir) and helping run the label Flood Music. Laurenzi is a saxophonist and a member of local combos such as Twin Talk, Edith Judith, and Natural Language, among others. He plays in Bill Callahan’s touring band and has contributed to recordings and live performances from Bon Iver, Macie Stewart, Jeff Parker, Japanese Breakfast, and many more. Gold and Laurenzi’s mesmerising new duo album, Devotional Fade, demonstrates why they’re both in such high demand. Its eight electroacoustic instrumental tracks display the duo’s creativity, skill, and musical chemistry in their oscillations between serene atmospheres and percolating rhythms.

Laurenzi and Gold developed the material on Devotional Fade during a month of weekly sessions, where they just let the tape roll the entire time. Laurenzi played tenor sax, clarinet, and synths, while Gold added electric bass, percussion, and drum machine. The title track opens the record on a subtle, meditative note, and even the busy percussion on “Clown Car” sounds relaxed—though blurry honking sounds pop up toward the end of the track, even then it feels less like a dinky clown car and more like an old Cadillac convertible, with space for everybody to spread out during meandering top-down rides. The bubbling, radiant “Soft Hold” drips and shimmers with electronics that play off Gold’s grooving guitar, and album closer “End of the Horn” combines hip-shaking rhythms and a dusky saxophone solo to suggest an al fresco celebration with plenty of dancing. Laurenzi and Gold are experts at building moods, and this album-release show ought to be a vibe.

The Moviegoer is the diary of a local film buff, collecting the best of what Chicago’s independent and underground film scene has to offer.

The first iteration of Beyond Chicago, an expansion of the LA-based genre festival, took place at the Music Box Theatre from April 2–5. It seemed to be a big hit; the Music Box posted on social media on Friday that every showtime had sold out.

On Saturday, I went to the fest’s double feature of Toshiya Fujita’s Lady Snowblood (1973) and Shunya Itō’s Female Prisoner Scorpion: Jailhouse 41 (1972), with Meiko Kaji, the star of both films, there in person. At 79 years old, she’s still a standout in any room; this theater, especially, was happy to see her, and even happier to see her shoot off a T-shirt cannon before each of the films. She was having a great time—her joy was infectious. She joked that this kind of adulation would keep her going for another ten years.

Still from Female Prisoner Scorpion: Jailhouse 41 (1972) Credit: courtesy Mubi

I was already really glad to have watched the films, in which Kaji stars as a strong woman in unusual predicaments. In the iconic Lady Snowblood, Kaji plays the titular character, a young woman avenging her family: Before her birth, her father and older brother had been killed, and her mother was sexually assaulted by some of the perpetrators. The latter exacted her revenge against one of them, which landed her in jail, where our heroine was born. She continues her mother’s quest for vengeance, first training to become a formidable assailant and then beginning to track down the others who murdered her family. The film was a major influence on Quentin Tarantino’s Kill Bill films, but Fujita’s is arguably better. It’s a strikingly beautiful film; Masaki Tamura’s cinematography is stunning, its gore rendered exquisitely.

Though Lady Snowblood is the better known of the two films, I was particularly drawn to Female Prisoner Scorpion: Jailhouse 41 (the second of four Female Prisoner Scorpion movies). Kaji remarked beforehand that she accepted the role as Nami Matsushima, also known as Matsu the Scorpion, on the contingency that she could play it mostly silent. The effect is brilliant, in large part due to Kaji’s acting—she conveys as much through a furrowed brow or observant glance as any words could. In terms of genre, it’s what’s known as a pinky violence film, which could be described as the Japanese corollary to sexploitation films with a bad-girl action component. (It’s related to pink films, which are more straightforwardly erotic.) The plot centers on a group of female prisoners who break out of jail. It’s surprisingly nuanced in its attitude toward these women, suggesting a level of ruthlessness that’s shocking but also empathy in regard to their circumstances and society’s view of them.

“No director could re-create the horror of Gaza.” A woman says this in Hala Bou Saab’s 2025 documentary The Miracle of Gaza; the titular miracle is her daughter, Halmia, who, at six years old, was presumed dead following an Israeli air strike. She remained in the morgue for several hours and was even prepared for burial before someone noticed her hand moving. In tones as straightforward as if they were discussing the weather, medical staff and family explain that her head injury was so severe that her brain was falling out of her skull. For them, such horrors are, tragically, as commonplace as the seasons, and are spoken of accordingly.

The Chicago Palestine Film Festival, founded in 2001, always features a robust lineup of documentaries that present necessary images of the suffering inflicted upon Palestine by Israel and the United States. Such films act as both witness and guide, providing context for an inarguably complex but woefully underilluminated crisis, with images and information working hand in hand. What stood out to me in several films from this year’s edition (though I did not preview all of them, so this is not definitive) are the stories that don’t focus on the current nature of the conflict. Perhaps in part because they went into production before October 7, 2023, such films instead foreground another central narrative in which the genocide simply plays a part. It’s like a film set during COVID where the pandemic is ever-present but not the subject. (It’s a sad but apt parallel that the occupation of Palestine is like a pandemic.)

Still from Thank You for Banking with Us! (2024)

Credit: courtesy Chicago Palestine Film Festival

This describes two of my favorite films that I watched: Thank You for Banking with Us! (2024) and Passing Dreams (2024), both set and shot in Palestine. In the former, screening Friday, April 17, at 8:30 PM, two estranged sisters come together after the death of their father to prevent their brother from inheriting more than them, as laid out by Islamic Sharia law. The older sister is a straightlaced stay-at-home mom; the younger is a single aesthetician with more relaxed values. Both supported their father in his final years, while their brother lives in America, which is why the sisters seek to secure their fair share of the inheritance. It becomes a comedy of errors when the sisters search for a man to pretend to be their now-dead father so that the bank will release his funds. The film is well directed and nicely shot, and the actresses who play the sisters, Clara Khoury (who will be in attendance for opening remarks) and Yasmine Al Massri, are fantastic. In an interview with Variety, director Laila Abbas noted that she didn’t “set out to criticize my people as if the West is the model to follow. . . . I am very critical of the West, and I love my country, which is why I’ve made this film, to have a conversation amongst ourselves and our society about what we aspire to be and how we need to evolve into something that looks like us.”

Though the film is more a commentary on patriarchal culture, it is nevertheless set against the backdrop of the occupation. Conceived before the events spurring the most recent genocide, Abbas admits, “I feel like I need to introduce the film and say we shot it before the war. I am not ashamed to tell a story that isn’t about the war, but there is something happening right now that is much more important than my film, and I need to talk about it.”

In Passing Dreams, which screens Saturday, April 18, at 8:30 PM, the occupation serves as the backdrop to a young boy’s quest for his beloved carrier pigeon, effectively becoming a metaphor for the Palestinian people themselves, hoping one day to be able to fly free. A road movie of sorts, the boy travels with his uncle and cousin across several locations in the occupied territories to find the bird’s original owner, to whom they believe it returned. Production-wise, it’s an impressive feat, shot in the actual locations where the story takes place and thus recognizable to Palestinians as geographically accurate. As director Rashid Masharawi also told Variety, “They know these places; what road they would have to take and the checkpoints. I don’t want to make shots like postcards. I want to be practical, going from A to B and showing a landscape. I was between showing the beauty but not exploring it like a tourist, even though I was in Bethlehem, one of the most important tourist sites in the world. Our characters just pass by because they’re on their way somewhere else.” The combination of the young characters and the world-weary uncle recalls the films of Abbas Kiarostami.

Another of the narrative offerings is Once Upon a Time in Gaza (2025), screening Tuesday, April 14, at 8:30 PM. The film premiered in the Un Certain Regard section of last year’s Cannes Film Festival, where it won the Best Director prize. Strikingly shot by Christophe Graillot, its plot is nevertheless more aimless than the previous two, though still worth seeing. In it, a student works at the falafel shop of a charming drug dealer who is later killed by a corrupt police officer. Several years later, the student is recruited to star in Palestine’s first action movie as an exalted martyr whom he resembles. This brings him into contact with the same police officer. It’s an interesting concept and undoubtedly the most unique way the ongoing conflict is situated within a generally unrelated central narrative.
