The documentaries are, of course, as illuminating as ever. The aforementioned The Miracle of Gaza screens Sunday, April 12, at 1 PM; it’s absolutely harrowing and heartbreaking, a stark reminder of who the world’s violence impacts most. Opening the festival is Traces of Home (2025), which screens Saturday, April 11, at 7 PM and Tuesday, April 28, at 6 PM. Director Colette Ghunim is the cofounder of the locally based Mezcla Media Collective; Kartemquin Films coproduced the documentary. In it, Ghunim travels with her parents to their respective homelands, Mexico and Palestine, to visit the homes they fled as children. It’s devastatingly intimate but likewise universal, as it explores themes of displacement, identity, and the concept of home.

Gaza Surf Club (2016), a documentary screened during a Chicago Palestine Film Festival several years ago, has stuck with me ever since. We are so besieged with images of pain and terror that it can be easy to forget that these aren’t just people, but individuals with interests such as surfing or even comedy. The latter is explored in Palestine Comedy Club (2025), screening Sunday, April 19, at 1 PM and again on Thursday, April 30, at 6 PM. The documentary follows six Palestinian stand-up comics as they travel around the occupied territories, and eventually beyond them, to perform. I was reminded of To Be or Not to Be (1942), wherein stars of a Warsaw theater troupe become embroiled in the resistance. It’s serious subject matter rendered wry by Ernst Lubitsch’s famous touch. The comedians in Palestine Comedy Club embody a similar spirit, not necessarily to laugh in the face of danger, but in spite of it. While some of the specificities of their Arabic-language-based comedy didn’t resonate with me (not for lack of comedy but of understanding on my part), the universal language of humor still translated.

The necessity for this abundance is sad, but the conviction with which the filmmakers and festival organizers provide it is hopeful.

Closing out the festival is American Doctor (2026), screening on Saturday, April 25, at 7 PM, with an encore screening on Sunday, April 26, at 12:15 PM. It follows three American doctors of differing backgrounds—Palestinian, Jewish, and Zoroastrian—as they work to save lives in Gaza and to influence international recognition of the ongoing genocide beyond it. Among the heroes of this moment are the doctors, from Palestine and around the world, who work ceaselessly to save lives with limited resources. This is evident as well in The Miracle of Gaza; it’s life-affirming in the most literal way to see the struggle for survival where it’s beginning to feel impossible. The filmmaker, as well as the three subjects—one of whom is Chicago-based—will appear in person for a postscreening Q&A following the Saturday screening, though it is sold out. But if there were any justice in the world, it would be these types of people whom the masses clamor to see, to hear their eyewitness accounts of preventable tragedies. For now, a sold-out screening will have to do.

Still from The Miracle of Gaza (2025)

Credit: courtesy Chicago Palestine Film Festival

Each of the films in the festival has something unique to offer in terms of story or information, or both; the necessity for this abundance is sad, but the conviction with which the filmmakers and festival organizers provide it is hopeful. Perhaps a director couldn’t re-create the horror of Gaza, but they can, more pointedly, show it.

Alice Maio Mackay is 21, and The Serpent’s Skin is her sixth feature. Like all her films to date, it offers a cohesive combination of genre, politics, and emotion.

Anna (Alexandra McVicker) is a trans girl who leaves her small-town home and abusive stepfather to go live in the city with her older sister. The day she moves in, she hooks up with the hot neighbor boy, and the next day she finds herself a job at a cool record store.

But everything isn’t perfect in the city. In the middle of her training, a man attacks her and attempts to rob the store. Attempts and fails—because Anna has powers. Mackay wisely never dives deep on lore, instead allowing fellow girl-with-powers Gen (Avalon Fast) to offer “They used to call us witches” as sufficient explanation for their abilities. As with many stories about young people with supernatural talents, the movie takes the two young women—who quickly fall for each other—down a difficult road when they unleash something unexpected.

From there, The Serpent’s Skin plays out almost like Buffy the Vampire Slayer if Buffy were a bisexual doll and we got to see her have erotically shot sex with men and women. There are scenes of all too real sister conflict built on care and concern, comfortable hangout scenes with friends, an enemy with a bumpy brow (a direct reference to Buffy’s vampire makeup), and a very good dose of genuinely affecting queer romance.

It’s a beautiful film, emotionally and aesthetically (cinematographer Aaron Schuppan and colorist Jessica Dunn Rovinelli do lovely work throughout), one that fits right in among the other sure-to-be cult classics in Mackay’s ever-growing oeuvre. 83 min.

August Wilson’s Ma Rainey’s Black Bottom was first produced at the Goodman in 1997, and the theater went on to be the first in the United States to produce all ten of the plays in Wilson’s acclaimed Century Cycle of dramas, each examining Black life in a different decade of the 20th century. Chuck Smith directed that earlier Goodman production, and Harry J. Lennix played Levee, the restless horn player in Ma Rainey’s band who wants to move beyond what he calls the “jug band” backing up the mercurial blues singer into the brighter and faster world of jazz.

Ma Rainey’s Black Bottom

Through 5/3: Wed 7:30 PM, Thu 2 and 7:30 PM, Fri 7:30 PM, Sat 2 and 7:30 PM, Sun 2 PM; also Sun 4/12 7:30 PM; ASL interpretation Fri 4/17 7:30 PM, audio description and touch tour Sat 4/18 2 PM (touch tour 12:30 PM), Spanish subtitles Sat 4/18 7:30 PM, open captions Sun 4/19 2 PM; Goodman Theatre, 170 N. Dearborn, 312-443-3800, goodmantheatre.org, $44-$109, 14+

Set in a Chicago recording studio in 1927, Ma Rainey’s Black Bottom was turned into a film in 2020 by director George C. Wolfe, using Ruben Santiago-Hudson’s adaptation of Wilson’s play (the playwright died at 60 in 2005). The film is fine (it won Oscar nominations for Viola Davis and the late Chadwick Boseman), but since I somehow had never managed to see the play onstage, I was delighted to see a Goodman revival announced last year. Now that I’ve seen the production (directed once again by the legendary Smith, with Lennix stepping offstage into the role of associate and music director), I’m even more delighted and stirred by what Smith and his astronomically gifted ensemble have done with Wilson’s story.

The real Ma Rainey was born Gertrude Pridgett in 1886, and with her husband, Will “Pa” Rainey, toured the Black vaudeville circuit. Her early blues recordings, including the song that gives Wilson’s play its title and “Moonshine Blues,” became early standards. Wilson takes liberties with her biography, but as played by E. Faye Butler, this Ma is all “Madame Rainey,” as she insists upon being called. Imperious, fierce, and aware of both her towering talents and the fragility of a career for an aging Black woman in a world dominated by greedy white producers, Butler’s Ma makes it clear that her defiance is a defense mechanism, with the studio manager, Irvin (Marc Grapey), most often on the receiving end of her tirades.

When Ma complains about not having Cokes in the studio and insisting that she’s not singing a note until they’re on hand, it’s clear (as it so often is in Wilson’s plays) that it’s not about the physical object. It’s about what that object represents in terms of respect and one’s place in the world. Later in the play, Levee’s attachment to his new Florsheims transmutes into something with even more profound implications than Ma’s demands for a cold Coca-Cola.

But while Ma is the star of the studio, it’s Levee’s story that drives the action, and Al’Jaleel McGhee’s performance is not to be missed. McGhee peels back the complicated layers of the cocky young man who, despite his apparent illiteracy, is eager to sell the world (or at least Ma’s producer, Sturdyvant, played with manipulative exasperation by Matt DeCaro) on his talents. Among other things, he’s written a new arrangement of “Ma Rainey’s Black Bottom,” and there’s ongoing conflict between Levee, Ma, and the other three members of the band about using it.

Ma wants to stick with what she knows, and the rest of the band—bassist Slow Drag (Cedric Young), pianist Toledo (Kelvin Roston Jr.), and trombonist Cutler (David Alan Anderson)—want to get on with the recording and collect their pay (hopefully in cold hard currency, as it’s too hard for them to cash a check). They’re also exasperated that Ma insists on giving her stuttering nephew, Sylvester (Jabari Khaliq), a job delivering the spoken intro to the title song, which puts them even further behind schedule as he struggles to get the lines out.

The conversations among the four men as they cool their heels in the basement musicians’ room initially flows between easy teasing wit and just the faintest sense of menace. Linda Buchanan’s adept set design establishes the physical hierarchy, with Sturdyvant dictating from on high in the booth, Ma and her younger girlfriend, Dussie Mae (Tiffany Renee Johnson), canoodling in the recording studio, and the musicians letting their guard down away from Ma and the white bosses in the basement. In his introduction, Wilson wrote that, for blues musicians, “This music often lies at the forefront of their conscience and concerns. Thus they are laid open to be consumed by it; its warmth and redress, its braggadocio and roughly poignant comments, its vision and prayer, which would instruct and allow them to reconnect, to reassemble and gird up for the next battle in which they would be both victim and the ten thousand slain.”

Warmth and braggadocio are both in plentiful supply, the latter coming out most plainly in the debates between Toledo, who prides himself on his book learning, and Levee. “You can’t even spell music, let alone play it,” Toledo needles Levee early on—and Levee proves him right. But sorrow enters the mix when Levee recounts a horrific story from his childhood in Natchez, Mississippi—an event that has made him question the existence of God ever since. Everything that came before in the play and everything that follows is, like the blues itself, refracted through that story of unimaginable pain and loss. Smith’s production connects the actors and the audience in an often spellbinding narrative that, though the story is set nearly a hundred years ago, still feels vital and urgent.

In addition to Butler and McGhee’s volcanic performances, the story is leavened and heightened by the deliberate but wise observations of Young’s Slow Drag, the acerbic asides of Anderson’s Cutler (who explodes at what he sees as Levee’s blasphemy), and the philosophical bent of Roston’s Toledo. “Everything changing all the time. Even the air you breathing change . . . changing all the time. Skin changing . . . different molecules and everything,” he observes, to which Levee retorts, “I’m talking about what I can see. I ain’t talking about no molecules or nothing.” The tragedy in Wilson’s play is that seeing doesn’t always lead to understanding until too late.

Smith, who has staged many Wilson plays over his distinguished career, knows how to let the spaces between the dialogue contract and expand to build camaraderie and tension. And though it takes Butler’s Ma a while to actually get around to singing, when she does, it’s a roof-raiser, distilling her own pain and resistance into a performance of raw vulnerability and knowing sensuality. A tour de force through and through, and one that shouldn’t be missed.

Cassandra or Kassandra: whichever way you spell the name of the famous (and famously ignored) prophetess of Troy, she’s having a (contemporized) moment on local stages. Eos Theatre Company is making their debut with Caroline Bird’s 2012 version of The Trojan Women (see review by Rob Silverman Ascher). And local playwright and Fat Theatre Project cofounder Eileen Tull brings her new one-act, Kassandra at the Top of the World, to life with her company in a coproduction (directed by Tull) with the Terror Cottas.

Kassandra at the Top of the World

Through 4/18: Wed–Sat 7 PM; Berger Park Coach House, 6205 N. Sheridan, theterrorcottas.org/projects/kassandra-at-the-top-of-the-world, $10 or pay what you can

The story of a woman who was dishonored and disbelieved looking at a world that is now on the verge of utter collapse hits pretty hard these days. “I told you so” can only provide so much comfort when, like Maya Moreau’s Kassandra in Tull’s story, you’re stuck on the top of a rock in the middle of a rapidly rising sea with only a trio of suspicious birds and your own tortured memories for company. “I warn, and I am worn,” she laments early on. She tries to befriend the birds with the bits of food she has left. “Barely any sustenance. I did not think that far ahead. Which is not something I say very often.”



Over 90 minutes, Kassandra recounts the story of her life in Troy as the overlooked daughter of King Priam and sister to Helenus (her twin, also a seer) and Hector—”the warner and the warrior.” Tull’s script is by turns poetic and sharp, laced through with sorrowful observations and epigrammatic turns of phrase on the cataclysmic effects of misogyny, war, and environmental depredation. (We’ve collectively been ignoring the climate Cassandras for decades now.) The trio of birds played by Jonathan Crabtree, Jacque Bischoff, and Joél Cordova offer comic relief and choral commentary.

The show does feel like it’s spinning its wheels from time to time, even though Moreau’s performance is focused and intense. The pacing feels overly deliberate, so while the story Kassandra is telling us is urgent, the elegiacal tone becomes a bit dirgelike. But when Ethan Carlson’s smug Apollo shows up, giving off vibes like Patrick Bateman in American Psycho, the story turns from the recursive recriminations and reflections of Kassandra’s tortured history to action. If humanity is to be saved, we need to kill our gods—and listen to women. That’s a message I can easily get behind.

Omnia Sol performs with Chicago A/V collective Veryveryvery at No Nation Art Lab. Credit: Courtesy Syd Ross

Syd Ross resists tidy categorization, but as an artist they’ve made contributions that echo throughout Chicago’s creative avant-garde. Ross, 35, has been vibrating in the city’s background since moving here in 2018: They’ve made signs for the Exchange in Wicker Park that look like video-game-themed crop circles, and they have a bit part in Monogamy House, a reality-show parody by Mitch Mitchell and Henry Hanson that’s easter-egged in Hanson’s 2022 cult masterpiece Bros Before. But Ross has really made noise with their work in the electronic-music community.

For a decade, Ross has been experimenting with the ideas and aesthetics underlying glitch art, especially in music. One of the factors that attracted them to Chicago was the presence of local artists working in glitch. Within that community, they work as Omnia Sol and run Heavy Shell Productions. During COVID lockdown, they began combining glitch video and music via an online show called The Omnia Sol Art Show, and when live music returned, they became a regular at Bridgeport venue DADS (Digital Art Demo Space), eventually getting booked regularly to provide live video for electronic musicians.

In 2023, aiming to refine their taste and skill in video art, Ross started grad school at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. They wanted to elevate the influence of the VJ by cultivating what they call the “cinematic rave,” a concept that reflects their appetite for media archaeology, cyborg feminism, plunderphonics and -optics, and comic books. Now they produce a show for CAN TV called Heavy Shell TV, which documents Ross’s creative experiments (especially with data moshing and risograph animation) and gives a platform to other groundbreaking electronic audio and video artists, all in a style that combines early MTV and cable access. They’ve also created audiovisual hybrid projects, most recently the four-song EP Head of Mars (released via Chicago label NFC), which they celebrated at No Nation Art Lab with a night of technology-driven art that defies format and genre. At the heart of Ross’s practice is an enthusiasm for remixing and cybernetics—not just as a style but as a political calling.

As told to Micco Caporale

I started HRT not last January 6 but the January 6 before that. So 2024. I did that so I’d never forget. It’s like 9/11 but much stupider.

I’m influenced by cyborg feminism. We’re already so entwined with technology—we already are cyborgs. We have the phone as an extension of us, the car as an extension of our feet. I don’t think technology is this absolute thing that’s going to save us, but I do think it’s intrinsic. What are we: humans or past that?

I’m from Springfield, Illinois. In high school, I wasn’t a very great student. I always had very bad ADHD, but back then they diagnosed it as executive function disorder, which is terminology they don’t use anymore. We’re all kind of under the AuDHD umbrella now, because there’s so many shared symptoms. But yeah, I was diagnosed with executive function disorder and really struggled in classes. It wasn’t until my junior year, when I went to a vocational school for graphic design, that I started to get better at school. Half the day I would work on the creatively focused things I wanted to do, and that gave me more time to do my homework for my regular classes.

In 2009, I went to Southern Illinois University in Carbondale. I originally went for graphic design, but I quickly realized I was too strongheaded about what I wanted to make. I was getting into alternative comics, always going to the library and checking out those Best American Comics collections. One that really stuck out to me was this one [by Paper Rad] called “Kramers Ergot [9 ‘Fuck You’],” which was about Kramer [from Seinfeld] having hallucinogenic experiences from eating moldy bread. I just thought that was great.



I had taken a few printmaking classes, and the head of the printmaking department, Travis Janssen, was great about knowing what his students wanted to do and helping guide them. He showed me comics’ relationship to silent film and the relationship between comics and printmaking, like the wordless books by Frans Masereel and Lynd Ward. These artists were making proto–comic books by having one woodcut per page. I switched to printmaking and got really into making woodcut comics and zines.

The title card from an upcoming episode of Heavy Shell TV featuring an audiovisual performance by VenoSci at Omnia Sol’s Head of Mars release party

Credit: Courtesy Syd Ross

In 2016 I moved to Saint Louis with my friend Adam Turl, who is an amazing artist. He lives back in Carbondale now and has the Born Again Labor Museum, which is this really interesting, like, art-installation house thing with paintings and this whole mythology he’s made behind it.

But in 2016, we started the Dollar Art House in Saint Louis. It was supposed to be like a dollar store for art, but because of zoning issues, we didn’t want to risk calling attention to that. It was just Dollar Art House: a gallery and living space about being socialist artists who wanted to appeal more to working-class and DIY sensibilities. We were both in Socialist Alternative at the time, so we would do fundraisers and stuff there too. Adam and I had our rooms and studios on the third floor, and the second floor had the gallery.

In Saint Louis, I didn’t want to pay for Internet, so I would go to the Salvation Army and get VHS tapes, five for a dollar. They were definitely trying to get rid of them, because if you went up with four tapes, they were going to charge you four dollars. You had to go grab a fifth tape to get the deal, so I got a lot of VHS tapes that way. At this point, I was doing a lot of paintings, and I loved painting while listening to music with a VHS on mute at the same time. I love the part of ADHD about having, like, multiple inputs at the same time.

I first started exploring glitch around 2015 or ’16. There are a lot of different definitions of glitch. It’s all the things you’re not supposed to see behind technical systems. People can take that politically, like the concept of glitch feminism. That’s about everyone who isn’t supposed to be seen, like trans people—we exist as glitches in society.

Glitch art is taking that and putting it into an artistic setting, like static on a TV from no signal coming through the antenna. Companies who make TVs think you don’t want to see the visual noise that creates, so now they give you this blue screen of death to cover that up. But the glitch artist wants to show you the static. In that static, there’s [cosmic] microwave [background] radiation. Something like 1 percent of that radiation is the same radiation that proves the big bang. There’s this strange spirituality to me about glitch.

It’s been about ten years of glitch, but I was mainly focused on digital glitch and specifically still images, like taking a photo and messing with the code. I loved taking image files and bringing them into sound software, like Audacity, then applying different effects to the raw data, seeing what it sounded like—which was very much harsh noise—and then exporting that again as an image and seeing, like, the echo or reverb effects that I put on the audio visualized in the photo.

A CRT video installation by Omnia Sol, demonstrating the technique of dirty mixing, appears in Sizzle Reel: A Documentary About Documentation: In Progress. Credit: Courtesy Syd Ross

I moved to Chicago in 2018. Adam had left Saint Louis, and I had been burglarized a couple times. In the back of my head, I’d always thought Chicago would be my next or final destination, but I always got stuck at a red light. It was taking forever. I was at a traumatic stage in my life and not happy, so I said, “Let me completely uproot my life and start something new.” But that paid off. I feel like I’m home.

Glitch has a huge history in Chicago. After moving here, Mitch Mitchell turned me onto the concept of glitchcraft, which is a combination of “glitch” and “witchcraft.” If you opened [an image] as a file and messed with the code, you could write your spell or intention into the code and see what happens. That was a really cool thing to explore both aesthetically and creatively.

During the pandemic, I was exploring video art. I had more free time and money than I was used to, and I had seen this artist in Portland posting about Big Pauper Modified Circuitry or BPMC. He makes these analog glitch devices for video art. Mitch Mitchell and I ended up splitting the cost of one, which was a Fluxus Duo. The main component is a dirty mixer, which is actually pretty easy to make yourself. If you’re looking at the A/V cord of an old VCR or game system or DVD player, you’ve got the white and red cords, which are your sound, and the yellow cord, which is your video. A dirty mixer takes two of those video signals and then has a knob or potentiometer between them that you can turn to one side or the other. When it’s sent to [a] CRT [television], the video will begin to slash and get very distorted. So it’s not a clean mix; it’s a dirty mix.

I originally wanted to do livestreams on Twitch, like a pirate radio station but with video, but I quickly found out how strict the YouTube bots are about blocking music. I was like, “I’ve got plenty of friends who are musicians. I’m just gonna get them to provide music and promote them.”

When I started doing The Omnia Sol Art Show, it was a lot of me talking, and I was very influenced by early vaporwave and Daniel Lopatin [aka Oneohtrix Point Never]. I love rap music too. A huge influence on that was DJ Screw, which I think also had a huge influence on vaporwave. DJ Screw had a dedication to analog. He would take these recordings—like cassette tapes—and slow them down and rerecord them with all the static and fuzz. [Vaporwave artists] were taking this technique of chopping and screwing but doing it with, like, elevator music and random commercial sounds.

Video still from the Head of Mars risograph animation by Omnia Sol Credit: Courtesy Syd Ross

Discovering video-art stuff got me doing live visuals for raves, which got me way more into electronic music and its history in Chicago. Electronic music was the first place that I was invited into with my art. There’s so many different subsets of electronic shows you could go to here, like a certain type of techno that’s a completely different vibe than another.

There’s techno for people who wear, like, Abercrombie & Fitch, and then there’s electronic music—like breakcore and everything—for people still wearing Tripp pants. I’m definitely not on the Abercrombie & Fitch side, even though I do have a perfect view of it from my window right now.

I think my style of video art goes hand in hand with nostalgic media archaeology. VHS fans, a lot of times, if they’re not steeped in the 80s horror vibe, they’re looking for anime tapes and that sort of thing. They’re interested in JRPGs [Japanese role-playing games] and video games, which leads you into chiptune, which was the first subgenre of electronic music that I VJed for. It’s a celebration of video game music, but it uses video games as instruments, like a Game Boy with this program called LSDJ [Little Sound Dj] that uses the Game Boy’s sound cards to make music in real time.

Early chiptune was doing what video artists like me were doing, but sonically instead of visually. My old setup was very chiptune and analog. I’d come in with two VCRs and a bunch of VHS tapes that I had dubbed with, like, anime, tokusatsu, and Japanese special-effects TV shows and glitch them in real time.

Risograph animation by Omnia Sol Credit: Courtesy Syd Ross

In 2022, I applied to SAIC for grad school. I really didn’t know what I was doing with my life, but I knew I had this passion for video art. I taught myself the technical aspects behind it, but it was such a steep learning curve not knowing about the history of video art or the amazing video artists that came before me, like Nam June Paik.

SAIC was the only school I applied to. I wanted to take this abstract glitch and put it in a more cinematic setting, and I knew they had a new-media program. I took a tour and saw their Sandin Image Processor, which was one of the first video synthesizers. It was developed in Chicago. I didn’t know there was such an interesting history here, but I knew there was a lot I couldn’t teach myself. I learned more in, like, two classes with James Connolly at SAIC than I did in two years trying to teach myself.

I have a screen-based practice, and one of my goals was to see my art in a movie theater. Going to the movies is so different from watching a movie at home, where there’s a million distractions. It’s a communal environment, with the lights low, and everyone’s focus is directed at the screen. You’re not supposed to be on your phone. It’s sacred to me. In grad school, I felt what I’d been exploring with wordless comics and printmaking come back.

I was thinking about silent filmmaking as a performance or a shared experience between a moving-image artist, live musicians, and an audience. The first VJ is the projectionist. Obviously the projectionist is not the filmmaker, but in that moment, the projectionist is the film artist, the handler of the film. We used to dance facing each other, and now, for better or worse, we’re all facing the DJ. The VJ gives us more to look at. You’re helping set the vibe and making the DJ look good by projecting these visuals behind them. But I’m interested in video and audio working in synergy, similar to the projectionist and the live orchestration during a silent film. I came up with this term “cinematic rave” to describe what I’m exploring.

My second year at SAIC I advised with Conor Stechschulte to find a way to bridge the gap between the video work I was doing and my desire to get back into prints and comics. He was a risograph professor who’s a published cartoonist. I ended up taking his deep risography class my last semester and using risograph animation in my thesis film, 100% Authentic Bootleg.

Omnia Sol’s film and visual album 100% Authentic Bootleg

I want to eventually make a short film that’s all risograph animation. I’m drawn to its tangibility. You have this print that you can see frame by frame, and then you have the actual moving image, similar to when you look at actual film and light being projected through celluloid. There’s also the tangibility of the textures that I’m able to create. It’s reminiscent of film grain to me.

100% Authentic Bootleg was originally going to be called Omnia Sol vs. Megalon, because I’ve done so much with tokusatsu footage. I’m very interested in remix culture, plunderphonics, and plunderoptics. I had done an album before called MKUltraman—a visual album specifically made for TikTok, where I took the entire album but shot it vertically, broke it up into one-minute segments, and uploaded it to TikTok. It was all glitched Ultraman footage. I wanted to make a sequel to that called Omnia Sol vs. Megalon that exclusively used footage from Godzilla vs. Megalon, because it’s one of my favorite Godzilla movies. It’s the perfect level of camp, but it’s also just awesome. But I noticed, whenever I worked with Godzilla footage, it got flagged. I was like, “Why is Toho so defensive of their IP?” Omnia Sol originally uploaded this 2022 album to TikTok as a series one one-minute vertical videos. It goes back to specifically this film, Godzilla vs. Megalon. There was a misunderstanding that it was in the public domain when it was not. When the dub came to the U.S., they forgot to put the copyright notice under the English titles, even though it was copyrighted in the Japanese titles. Everyone thought it was similar to Night of the Living Dead, where they left off the copyrights so it was immediately put into public domain. Everyone put out VHS bootlegs of Godzilla vs. Megalon. I became really fascinated by that.

Omnia Sol vs. Megalon morphed into my film and album 100% Authentic Bootleg, which is the same concept of glitching Godzilla vs. Megalon footage. There are a lot of deeper themes in the film that are not explored before we get to these men in costumes essentially doing tag-team wrestling. But the main antagonist, Megalon, wasn’t like Godzilla, who came out of the ocean. There was an underground society called Seatopia, who were tired of nuclear tests affecting their habitat, so they did this ritual to raise this beetle god, Megalon, to attack the surface world.

Then scientists make this robot, Jet Jaguar, who’s clearly an Ultraman rip-off. He’s stolen by the citizens of Seatopia, who reprogram him to fight alongside Megalon, but then he spontaneously gets intelligence and fights alongside Godzilla? I wanted to highlight that underlying narrative about spirituality and the environment as well as the role of AI and all these cybernetic themes.

A clip from episode 14 of Heavy Shell TV that demonstrates the technique of data moshing Credit: Courtesy Syd Ross

I originally was trying to put 100% Authentic Bootleg out on my friend’s label, Mobcore, which is a breakcore DIY label in Chicago that’s big on not selling anything. Since I was doing a VHS, they’re like, “Maybe we could put out a free EP down the line, but you should put this out on your own.” I had already edited it to say “Mobcore Records present . . . ,” so I had to swap it out.

Being really into tokusatsu, I was watching a lot of Juukou B-Fighter, which was the footage used for Big Bad Beetleborgs in the U.S., kind of similar to how they took Super Sentai and turned it into Power Rangers. “Juukou B-Fighter” translates to “Heavy Shell B-Fighter,” and I really liked that term: heavy shell. Has a nice mouthfeel. So I started Heavy Shell Productions. My artist name is Omnia Sol, but if I’m putting out a film or zine or VHS, it’s going to be under Heavy Shell Productions.

After grad school I wanted to bring The Omnia Sol Art Show back in a new form. I was introduced to this guy Lucas [Herzog] who works at CAN TV, who suggested I submit something, and that became Heavy Shell TV. I did 12 episodes last year, and season two is coming up. Heavy Shell TV puts more emphasis on documenting my audiovisual performances, but I try to really emphasize the music-video aspect of it, down to the way I credit the songs. I’m trying to re-create that old MTV thing—like, this is how you find new bands or rappers or whatever. It’s similar to the VJ being the person behind the scenes emphasizing the DJ and making them look good.

The EP I just released is called Head of Mars. The cover was taken at the Art Institute of this sculpture of the head of the god Mars. I was thinking about the current state of the world and the endless wars we seem to be in. I had done a project in grad school called Overview that was very much about the earth and Gaia, and I had used the Orphic hymn to Gaia.

Footage of the Omnia Sol installation Overview from 2024

I read through the Orphic hymn to Ares, and there was a really interesting part that mimics this verse in Isaiah about turning weapons into plowshares. You’re calling upon Ares, this god of war, but for a time of peace where war is not needed. That was an emphasis for me, with the visuals and aggressive sounds—this emphasis of, like, “No war but class war.” I brought in the sci-fi aspects of Mars, with a lot of samples from different animes, like Gundams and Macross. There’s also this interesting Taiwanese movie I found called Mars Men that’s all these different kaiju fighting each other on Mars.

I have one song that’s called “On Time” that samples this old Soviet record. I don’t speak Russian, but it’s a very beautiful, dramatic song. I was originally going to try to sample it by taking the seven-inch record and playing it at 33 rpm instead of 45. What I didn’t know is that Soviet seven-inches were actually put out at 33 rpm, not 45, so you could fit more music on it. To get that slowed-down sound, I ended up just putting my hand on the vinyl and manually slowing it down to record and sample it that way. The song takes a lot of that, and breakcore and breakbeat drums that are chopped up.

The last song on Head of Mars gets a bit jam-bandy in that space-rock-era way. I used samples of Soviet synthesizers, which are very spacey. We developed electronic music very differently than the Soviets. A Soviet factory would be making weapons and have leftover material, like, “Well, we don’t want to waste anything.” So you have all these old Soviet synthesizers and guitar pedals that are really good quality metal and made not to fall apart.

[My approach] is similar to how early Kraftwerk took a lot of influence from the Soviet avant-garde and this optimism about a future after the revolution. I want to explore that in a media archaeology setting. We’re so far removed from that now. It feels nihilistic and bleak. I always go back to [that quote in Mark Fisher’s book Capitalist Realism]: “It’s easier to imagine the end of the world than the end of capitalism.” The capitalists are more willing to let the world die than they are to change anything.

My friend Adam Turl had this grad-school project called “Red Mars” that was influential on the album. It was a sci-fi story told through a collection of paintings. After the capitalist class escapes to Mars, they leave us behind, but eventually there’s a revolution. It might be led by robots—whoever the new working class is. It’s imagining solidarity with robots of the future, not in a right-wing, Elon Musk way—in a proletariat-focused way.

The open decks at last year’s inaugural Chicago Electronic Music Conference Credit: Courtesy the Chicago Electronic Music Conference

The Chicago Electronic Music Conference debuted in 2025 at the Ramova Theatre, and for year number two it’s returning to the same venue on Saturday, April 11. Like any good music conference, CEMC will have a vendor hall (in this case loaded with DJ and synth gear), a record shop pop-up, and plenty of panels, workshops, and performances. Among the workshops are a lesson in advanced sound design by Dallas DJ producer Gvnnr (“Understanding LFOs, Envelopes & Modulation”) and a music business roundtable for independent artists.

The day’s panels include a discussion of the cultures built by dance music (featuring footwork veterans King Charles and Prince Jron, among others) and a look into the history and future of Chicago house music with key figures such as Lori Branch, Vince Lawrence, and DJ Hyperactive. (The latter is also on the bill at the CEMC afterparty.) The Ramova’s taproom hosts local DJs spinning all day, including Shanti of techno collective Research & Development, Podlasie regular J. Copes, and west-side boogie and disco lover Sunshine Rewind. The conference runs from noon till 10 PM, and tickets cost $52.51 in advance.

Ensemble dal Niente flutist Emma Hospelhorn also sings and plays guitar, bass, electronics, and keyboards, which has made her an in-demand support musician in contexts as varied as indie rock, folk, free improvisation, contemporary classical, and avant-garde sound art. She impressed Gossip Wolf in 2022 with her solo debut as Em Spel,The Carillon Towers, and she followed it up last month with the full-length Bird or Snake, which threads together tautly picked guitars, gently wafting flute, and lovely overdubbed vocal harmonies.

Hospelhorn gathered a rad collection of collaborators to help flesh out the new album’s experimental folk, including Katie Ernst (basses), Dustin Laurenzi (saxophone), Mabel Kwan (synth), Eric Ridder (drums), and Sam Wagster (pedal steel guitar). For the Bird or Snake release show at Constellation on Saturday, April 11, the Em Spel band will include all those musicians plus saxophonist Sarah Clausen. Ernst and Laurenzi will play an opening set as their folk duo, Edith Judith, joined guitarist Matt Gold for the occasion. Tickets cost $23.83, and the show starts at 8:30 PM.

Emma Hospelhorn created the detailed, inventive arrangements on Bird or Snake with help from seven other musicians.

Hospelhorn also maintains a duo with cellist Katinka Kleijn that’s focused on homemade circuits and orchestral instruments. Kleijn is a member of the Chicago Symphony Orchestra, which will bring one of her experiments to the stage at Orchestra Hall on Wednesday, April 8. The CSO describes Kleijn’s Bionic Synthmap as “a site-specific sound sculpture that explores shared circuits between human bodies and synthesizers.” The sculpture includes pieces of conductive material arranged on the floor in a large design, and when performers touch two of those pieces at once, they influence the configuration of the sound-making circuit. Kleijn will accompany the installation’s output with cello and projected visuals, and to close the night, she’ll invite audience members onstage to shape what they’re hearing firsthand. Tickets cost $30, and the event begins at 8 PM.

Cassette label LittleHeadButt is releasing the new Menace4Hire album on tape.

Local cassette label LittleHeadButt has been doing impressive work spotlighting underground sounds from Chicago and around the country. So far this year, the label has issued a nasty, unrelenting dance-noise EP called Northwest Territories by Seattle artist Baphomet Sex and a physical edition of the 2025 album Coming With the Strap by local art-punk project Bussy Kween Power Trip. On Saturday, April 11, LittleHeadButt hosts a release party at Cole’s for the cassette version of My Ancestor’s Favorite, a great jazz-inflected hip-hop album that underground Chicago MC Menace4Hire self-released digitally last month. The first album in six years from local hardcore crew Through N Through

Hard-hitting Little Village band Through N Through have been dispensing metal-tinged beatdown hardcore for roughly a decade. They hadn’t put out a full-length since 2019’s Our Side . . . till last week, when they dropped a self-titled album! On Thursday, April 9, they headline Cobra Lounge to celebrate the long-awaited arrival of Through N Through. Mictlan and Wrath Hammer open. Tickets cost $15, and the show kicks off at 7 PM.

Meet the Flyover Gals: Gertie’s Abby Pucker and Chanelle Lacy, alongside Mariane Ibrahim Gallery’s Emma McKee—three women rooted in Chicago’s art scene, sending back vivid dispatches from their art world journeys across the midwest. In this Chicago Reader series, the trio captures the creativity, grit, and unexpected beauty shaping the heartland’s cultural landscape.

We’ve all been sitting with the same question: We’re the third-largest metro in the country, so why do we so often act like a provincial city? Chicago is a world-class arts city. And yet this sentiment persists. As Carol Diehl wrote in 1990, “Chicago has long suffered from an inferiority complex, the sense that ‘if it’s from New York or Europe it must be better,’ that keeps it from realizing its potential.” That was 35 years ago.

We have the scale, the institutions, the creative energy. What we need is belief in ourselves. A scarcity mindset tells us there isn’t enough room, recognition, or relevance to go around, so we hoard, compete, and look elsewhere for validation. An abundance mindset does the opposite: It compounds. The more we champion each other, the more legitimacy we collectively build. Confidence is contagious, and it’s also a signal. How we project ourselves as a city with something to say is exactly how the rest of the world decides whether to listen.

That confidence shouldn’t stop at the city limits. The midwest is full of cities that are even more overlooked than we are, but have just as much to celebrate. We want to view the other places in the region as an extension of our strength—not as competition, but part of our larger context. When Chicago connects with Detroit, Cleveland, Minneapolis, we’re not diluting what makes us special—we’re building something larger, and truer, than any one city can hold.

Dispatches from the middle: Detroit

March 21-22, 2026

Detroit was the obvious city to highlight first. With EXPO Chicago upon us, we thought it would be good to visit some of the artists, galleries, and collectors that will be descending upon our fair city in just a few weeks. We saw this trip as the perfect opportunity to build new relationships, deepen existing ones, and start some conversations about programming.

Getting there: Drive or take the train and rent a car. You’ll fit in far more stops.

Getting around: Everything is basically 15 minutes away. Skip public transit and just drive or rideshare. This is the Motor City.

Where to stay: Splurge on the Shinola Hotel. The Siren Hotel is also great.

Our Detroit guide: There are few better guides to Detroit’s art world than Katie A. Pfohl, associate curator of contemporary art at the Detroit Institute of Arts (DIA). She’s also the curator of EXPO Chicago’s Focus section this year. Focus features almost 50 galleries, 12 years or younger, each displaying the work of one or two artists. Katie excitedly let us know that three Detroit galleries and six Detroit artists will be participating in EXPO.

A visit to Periodicals

Courtesy of the authors

Saturday, March 21, 2026

10 AM-10:30 AM: Visit to Periodicals with founder Aleiya Olu and Erica Jackson

We started the day at Periodicals, a magazine and concept shop founded by Aleiya Olu. Carrying local and international publications across art, politics, culture, and design, it’s a quietly radical space that feels especially urgent in a moment when access to information is increasingly contested. Also joining us was Chicago-raised, Detroit-based Erica Jackson, who spoke to the threads between the two cities. She’s currently building LIMITLESS, an intimate creative membership space opening within the year, centered on opportunities for local creatives across photography, programming, marketing, food, and hospitality.

11:20 AM-12:15 PM: Tour of the Shepherd followed by coffee and divine pastries at Warda

We met up with Library Street Collective’s senior director, Tara Akitt, for a tour of the Shepherd, where we were delighted to discover a satellite location of Periodicals tucked inside. Classic Detroit. The exhibition was curated by Allison Glenn (former gallery director at Chicago’s Monique Meloche), and after we ducked around the corner to Warda Patisserie for coffee and pastries with Erica.

Where Chicago can calcify around politics and gatekeeping, Detroit leads with invitation. The conversation centered on how the art world here extends well beyond museum walls into neighborhoods and civic life, and how many of Detroit’s most committed cultural figures have come from elsewhere. The city earns that loyalty by operating from a different posture entirely. Having built its community largely without government or corporate support, the instinct here is to bring people into the work.

1 PM: A visit to Lane and Leigh Coleman’s home and collection

Lane Coleman is the newly appointed (2024) board chair of DIA. Lane grew up in Chicago, and Leigh Coleman in Saint Louis; both made Detroit their home decades ago. They generously welcomed us with an extensive tour of their home and the art collection they have built over the years. The collection was peppered with names we recognized—and includes local Black artists spanning generations—but it was also marked by a genuine interest in building a global collection rooted deeply in the concepts that have shaped Detroit’s artistic movements.

4 PM: The Heidelberg Project

The Heidelberg Project is a conceptual art installation that Tyree Guyton has been building for decades. Part real estate investment, part public sculpture garden, part archival project—it’s marked by recurring visual themes like clocks drawn on trees or hung on branches. In Detroit, time isn’t linear but ecological: Things decompose and become substrate for what comes next. Our time with Tyree was whimsical, questions answered with more questions, punctuated by an improbable number of stories about nude beaches.

Detroit doesn’t wait to be discovered. It just creates, building its own ecosystem, welcoming anyone who wants to be part of it. We should take note.

The artist residency and community space Buffalo Prescott caters to caregivers.

Courtesy of the authors

5 PM: Buffalo Prescott

Katie brought us to Buffalo Prescott (BP), a residency and community space founded by Samara Furlong and co-led with Leto Rankine, built around supporting artists who are also caregivers, mostly working parents. Unlike traditional residencies, BP imposes no strict timelines, welcomes families and pets, and stays open 24/7. Samara and Leto also help artists navigate the business side of their practice. We asked for a price list on our way out and had it in our inboxes within the hour. A publishing arm rounds out the model, focused on building an archive of critical writing around each artist’s practice.

Their longer-term vision is a five-to-ten-year cultural exchange program that brings major exhibition-level art to Detroit, a city with a vibrant creative community but limited gallery infrastructure. A recent trip to Chicago crystallized it: “We realized there is not enough art coming into Detroit from outside,” Furlong said. The goal is to bring the world to Detroit and let Detroit inspire the world back. Their first move in that direction is a partnership with Casa Wabi, featuring artist Cristina Umaña, whose work they see in close dialogue with BP residents. Just another way that we feel like we’re rowing in the same direction as Detroit. “Chicago to the World and the World to Chicago” is Gertie’s unofficial tagline.

6:30 PM: Matéria visit with preview of EXPO works by Jova Lynne and Carole Harris

Katie dropped us off with Simone DeSousa at her gallery Matéria, which will have a booth at EXPO, before heading off to handle childcare. (Women really do do it all.) We saw the gallery’s multigenerational presentation of Jova Lynne and Carole Harris.

In Portuguese, Matéria means both physical substance and a subject of study, a duality that maps perfectly onto Simone’s identity as an artist and small business owner. Emma and Simone bonded immediately over a shared conviction: that running a contemporary gallery right now requires nothing short of superhuman resilience. Simone’s practice grew out of the community, in the spirit of artists who build their own spaces, a model intrinsic to the midwest. “Being a channel for things to take place, that’s my life practice,” Simone said. “How do you completely engage but not be attached to the outcome?” The act of starting something matters. The process always outweighs the result.

The day was capped with drinks at Kiesling.

Courtesy of the authors

7:30 PM: Drinks/Apps at Little Liberia Restaurant

Michigan’s first Liberian restaurant, Little Liberia, had just opened its doors. Chef Ameneh Marhaba founded it as a pop-up in 2016. We ate roasted wings with a garlic herb rub, collard greens with tender beef, and whole fried fish with dry rice. Our winner for the night was the collard greens.

9:45 PM: Signing off at Kiesling

Martinis galore. A great place to nest in a big booth and mentally, emotionally, and physically digest the day.

Sunday, March 22, 2026

9 AM: Shinola Hotel Coffee recap

Abby met up with Emma for breakfast at San Morello, situated right off the lobby. The perfect place to grab a coffee and some baked eggs before heading to the DIA to round off our trip.

The story of Detroit is inseparable from that of the Detroit Institute of Arts.

Courtesy of the authors

10 AM: Detroit Institute of Arts

The DIA’s story is inseparable from Detroit’s. The museum is working on a transformational new modern and contemporary wing, slated to open in late 2026.

Much of Detroit’s spirit is rooted in public ownership, embodied most clearly at the DIA. Katie told us about the institution’s history: The city owned the DIA’s art collection until it filed for bankruptcy in 2013, when citizens rallied to prevent the museum’s holdings from being liquidated. That near-crisis catalyzed a new model. The DIA became an independent nonprofit, with roughly 68 percent of the museum’s budget funded by a Tri-County property tax that has been renewed through 2032. In return, residents get free admission, and K–12 students can take free field trips. The DIA now carries no debt and is building toward a self-sustaining endowment.

Final thoughts

Beyond the walls of the institution where Katie spends much of her day working, she described a city where decades of ambition are finally finding their footing: “It really does feel like the moment where the work of many people over the course of many decades is finally coming to fruition—and you’re starting to see people do it with a real ethics of place.”

What makes Detroit distinctive, she explained, is that the creative community isn’t building in reaction to something; it’s building toward something. “You have this opportunity to imagine what you want to see—not in spite of anything, but in line with the city’s history of art, activism, and organizing.” And with fewer entrenched systems to push against, the imagination can run further: “Detroit provides this model of what it means to dream without having to push against lots of existing infrastructure.”

For Chicagoans, a day trip to Detroit is less about finding an alternative to what we have at home and more about finding a mirror. One that reflects some exciting possibilities for what cities like ours can become if we expand our idea of who we are and who gets to be part of the “Chicago art world.” Think of it as a short drive to visit a cousin you love and realize you haven’t kept up with nearly enough. After the trip, we vowed to see our cousins in Detroit more often because our lives are richer and stronger with them.

Playwright Itamar Moses won a Tony Award in 2018 for his book for The Band’s Visit—a lovely musical based on Eran Kolirin’s 2007 film about an Egyptian band that gets on the wrong bus on their way to a concert in Israel and spends the night bonding with the residents of the dusty town where they’re stranded. The musical, like the film, emphasizes the commonality between the Israelis and the Egyptians, with politics very much in the background.

That’s very much not the case for Moses’s 2024 play, The Ally, now in a local premiere at Theater Wit under Jeremy Wechsler’s direction, which explodes with rhetoric and recrimination—mostly around Israel and Palestine, but also touching on a host of other urgent issues. Wechsler also directed Joshua Harmon’s Prayer for the French Republic last spring at Northlight (a coproduction with Theater Wit), which looked at anti-Semitism through the generational experiences of a Jewish family in Paris, and also included a barrage of arguments over Jewish identity and responsibility.

The Ally

Through 5/17: Thu–Sat 7 PM, Sun 2 PM; also Sat Theater Wit, 1229 W. Belmont, 773-975-8150, theaterwit.org, $30-$44

Moses’s play (a finalist for the 2025 Pulitzer Prize in drama—the award went to Branden Jacobs-Jenkins’s Purpose, which started out at Steppenwolf) is pointedly set in September 2023. But though the horrific events of the last two and a half years aren’t addressed directly here, everything that has happened inevitably hangs over Moses’s story. One can certainly argue that stopping the action of the play just before October 7, 2023, is a way of copping out. But as in Harmon’s play, the point is that these conflicts are both evergreen and volatile. In the case of Moses’s story, the focus is on well-meaning people far away from most of the conflicts referenced in the play trying to figure out what it means to do the right thing.

That’s certainly the case for writer and very part-time university playwriting and screenwriting professor Asaf Sternheim (Jordan Shappell). Like Moses, Asaf is a fortysomething Berkeley-raised son of Israeli immigrants. He’s now living with his Korean American wife, Gwen Kim (K Chinthana Sotakoun), in a university town that feels suspiciously like University City in Philadelphia. Gwen is working a high-pressure administrative job in community relations, and is trying to sell the community on the university’s growth plans against the backdrop of a previous expansion that decimated Bottomville, a primarily Black neighborhood. (The neighborhood largely destroyed by Penn was known as “Black Bottom.”)

Asaf is approached by a Black former student, Baron Prince (DeVaughn Asante Loman), about signing a petition (a manifesto, really) written after Baron’s cousin, Deronte, was shot and killed by cops after being wrongly accused of stealing cars. He’s initially on board, even though it’s painfully clear that he hasn’t paid much attention to Deronte’s story (he somehow never saw the video that went viral after the murder). Gwen thinks his support of the Black community will also help her in her position selling them on the university expansion, even if she’s a little leery that Baron is working with lawyer and activist Nakia Clark (Sharyon Culberson), who happens to be Asaf’s former college girlfriend.

Early in the play, Asaf says, “Under the thin surface of Israeli-immigrant stoicism is plain old Jewish guilt.” That line becomes a harbinger of how Asaf moves through the increasingly explosive world of the play. He signs the petition, despite his discomfort upon reading the manifesto with language tying oppression of Black and Brown communities in the U.S. to Israeli treatment of Palestinians. He largely agrees with the points raised, but questions why Israel is the only country other than the U.S. to be called out by name for its oppression of others, noting that it doesn’t call for sanctions against China for its treatment of Tibetans or Uyghurs, or the Indian government for its attacks on Kashmir and Muslims. When Gwen asks him why he’s being defensive, Asaf replies, “I’m just defensive of internally consistent logic.”



That’s a big part of what’s on the table in Moses’s play. After signing the petition, Asaf agrees to sign on as a faculty sponsor of a new Jewish–Palestinian student group on campus, formed by American Jew Rachel Klein (Mira Kessler), a descendant of Shoah survivors, and Farid El Masry (Eliyah Ghaeini), a Palestinian born in Gaza who still has family in Palestine. Rachel and Farid formed their group to host a talk by an Israeli historian, Isaac Roth, who is highly critical of Israel, and whose appearance was denied support by the existing Jewish campus group to which Rachel previously belonged.

To Asaf, supporting the historian’s appearance is a free-speech issue. But his “acoustic-guitar-based variety of Judaism,” as he describes his progressive upbringing, goes through the wringer when he’s confronted by a Jewish grad student, Reuven Fisher (Evan Ozer), who accuses him of offering “a public self-flagellation, a performance of virtue for the goyim.”

Asaf’s doubts about what he’s doing with the student group come to a head when Baron goes onstage after Roth’s speech to call for divestment and sanctions against Israel, and the seeds laid in the first act burst into burning bushes in the second. Every character (even the arguably underwritten Gwen) gets their voices in, sideways or otherwise. (Though that underwriting may be emblematic of how Asian Americans are often elided from discussions about racism in the U.S.) Everyone has a strong point. Yet everyone is also, at various times, incapable of granting nuance and grace to others.

One could argue that these are problems that will inherently arise in broad-based social justice movements. People who believe in Israel’s right to exist can also be full-throated critics of police violence. Or, as Reuven does in talking about Deronte’s murder, they may fall prey to the racist narratives promoted by the cops. People who have known what displacement and discrimination (let alone genocide) mean can end up working for institutions or organizations that will cause others to experience the same horror.

If everything is connected, how do you negotiate a world where you believe firmly in this cause, but have questions about how it’s tied into that issue? And how, if all forms of oppression are connected, does it make sense to dismiss people’s concerns about an “unrelated” issue as “what-aboutism?” And when you have tangled and difficult personal history, as Nakia and Asaf do, how do you separate those emotions and memories from political debate?

These are just some of the heady and passionate questions embodied over the course of the two and a half hours of Moses’s play. It’s a play of ideas, but it’s not a dusty one. The cunning set by Joe Schermoly, which places us in a book-lined library, suggests the world of history and political philosophy surrounding the characters, and the high cathedral-like ceilings also suggest something elevated into the realm of pure intellectual and spiritual discourse—a realm that inevitably takes a beating when real people’s real experiences with racism, poverty, anti-Semitism, genocide, apartheid, gentrification, and so many other ugly things enter the sanctum and turn over the tables.

It’s a talky play and occasionally an exhausting one that inevitably reinvestigates arguments and narratives that have dominated progressive spheres over the past few years, especially. (The conservative spheres don’t seem to give a damn about the lives of anyone in the Middle East, as usual.) I won’t argue that anyone will come away from The Ally with a different point of view than they already held. But as the last scene between Asaf and a rabbi (Culberson) illustrates, separating feelings from ideas in itself leads to what she calls “a wall between our bodies and our minds,” pointing out that “all traumatized people do this, not just Jews.” Would we all be better off if we stopped talking past each other and just sat quietly in a room by ourselves once in a while to sort out that mind-body connection? Moses doesn’t exactly say that. But he’s not not saying it, either.

Wechsler’s cast, particularly Shappell and Ghaeini, are compelling to watch even when the discourse feels like it’s veering into occasional repetition. The latter’s monologue recounting all that has happened to Farid’s Palestinian family over the decades is one of the most wrenching moments in the production. For the most part, the actors avoid the trap of playing the self-righteous posturing at the expense of the doubt lying just under the surface of their words. Their words sound assured, but their reactions to each other illustrate their vulnerability.



It’s also often a very funny play, despite the subject matter. Seeing people acting out of motivations they don’t entirely understand is often a source of humor, onstage and off. Asaf, for all his good intentions, is mostly a guy who just wants to write his plays about the European Enlightenment and feel like a good person without being on the hot seat, which leads to awkward but hilarious moments of revelation. And by the end, you may find yourself wrestling again with the question of whether the multilayered and interconnected problems we face require more nuance—or if our search for nuance itself can be self-congratulatory, obscuring what people who believe they seek justice need to do.

I’m crouched like a vampire over the counter in my half-lit kitchen, wondering why I left the house yesterday. I haven’t slept in almost 24 hours, and my drooping flesh bag needs to drag itself back to the coffin before sunrise.

My brain has other ideas. Bad ideas. It wants to stay awake and relive the failures of the day as if that would bleed them out.

But there’s a cake in front of me. It glows in the dark—lavender-colored, fuchsia-speckled buttercream draped with inky purple jam. I stab it with a fork and push it into my mouth.

It rushes through me: a flood of orange chiffon, sticky berries, tart sumac, and as I swallow, and my eyes close, it bites me, a sting of chili so unexpected I laugh out loud.

And then I remember—someone gave me this cake hours earlier before everything went south. That unexpected gesture is why I left the house. I’d gone out where people were gathering to forget the horrors of the day with the unfailing alchemy of food and friendship.

It didn’t go to plan that evening, but that is the magic formula that’s sustained humankind for all of its existence. Weddings, parties, birthdays, funerals, harvest moons, holidays, send-offs, homecomings, divorce settlements, happy hours, mass vaccinations after prolonged periods of isolation, protests in opposition to fascism, or whatever occasion satisfies the primal need for human contact—they’re always fueled by food. Eating is the commonality that makes them work.

That’s what we go for at Monday Night Foodball, the Reader’s long-running weekly guest chef pop-up at Thattu in Avondale.

Credit: Henry Barret

This thing that started almost five years ago just finished its 2026 winter schedule on a low note. We’d gotten some good press recently, and it seemed to have spiked attendance. First-timers lined up and ordered food with the faithful regulars, sipping avocado martinis that tasted like milkshakes, and the party got started.

Then it got messy, disorganized, chaotic, frustrating. Mistakes were made. People got hangry, which almost never happens.

It was an unusually unhappy ending for a Foodball, compounded by the terrible first impression it made on the new folks. Normally, I wake up on Tuesdays feeling warm and fuzzy, but not this time. I felt hot and dreadful.

Later, I sat down with Thattu owners Chef Margaret Pak and Vinod Kalathil for a postmortem, and we raged at the perfect storm that hit the restaurant. Literally. The cherry on the shit sundae was a lightning strike in the alley early that morning after everyone left, temporarily knocking out the power.

Once we blew off steam generated by all the things that seemed out of our control, we made a plan to stormproof Mondays at Thattu.

Bison taco by Ketapanen Kitchen

Not that I expect any storms from the new spring lineup of badass chefs cooking everything from kitchen barbarian Basque, to Hawaiian-Filipino, Nigerian, Mexican, Indigenous, Guatemalan, yinzer red sauce Italian, and Silk Road–spiced French pastry.

It all starts Monday, April 13, with a lysergic union of culinary forces: the return of Jeremy Leven’s Basque-inspired Gilda, with veteran Foodball weirdos Rafa Esparza and Anthony Baier’s FAFO, just ahead of the opening of their new West Town brick-and-mortar.

Then on 4/20, it’s Roland Floro Calupe’s Pacific Island–hopping Panlasa, followed by a West African jollof party with Dozzy Ibekwe’s Dozzy’s Grill on April 27.

On Quatro de Mayo, it’s a street vendor buyout in collaboration with the Street Vendors Association of Chicago, followed by Guatemalan street food from Thattu line cook Shirley Cisnero’s Margot’s Fusion Kitchen.

Jessica Walks First’s all-Indigenous Ketapanen Kitchen returns for her fifth (and possibly last) Foodball on May 18, one week before the Memorial Day break. Then restaurant PR guru Dave Andrews launches his Pittsburgh red sauce Italian project Macerelli’s, on June 1, the feast day of Saint Fortunatus of Spoleto, n’at.

I’m not promising Windy City Burger Social Club’s Anas Masoud will do that cheesesteak when he comes back on June 8, but I will encourage it.

The long-awaited return of Milo’s Market from homie Berto Bahena on June 15 proves he isn’t too big to grill me a quesabeeria after all.

And then a three-peat from Best of Chicago pastry pop-up winner and aforementioned cake angel Divs Ray and her Umami from Scratch on the second day of summer, June 22.

It winds up with the premiere of reimagined classical Cantonese from Chicago restaurant royalty: Carol Cheung of the late, great Jade Court on June 29.

Fletcher in Avondale on April 13 at 5 PM for happy hour, with $5 beers and nonalcoholic drinks, and $12 bespoke cocktails by Melanie Hernandez. EXPO Chicago—our city’s premier art fair, now in its 13th edition—returns this week, bringing with it gallerists, collectors, and art enthusiasts from around the globe.

Much ado has been made about the downsizing of this year’s fair—the first under the direction of Kate Sierzputowski and the third since Frieze acquired it. The number of participating galleries has dropped from around 170 to around 130, and EXPO has excised the Special Exhibitions and Editions + Books sections, which typically featured many local institutions. Still, there will be 12 local galleries with official presentations at the fair. And perhaps the smaller size will make the fair feel less exhausting.

It’s also worth remembering that EXPO Chicago is a commercial enterprise, and is perhaps not your best bet for discovering the most exciting local artists or learning about the coolest art spaces. Fortunately, EXPO Art Week helps draw attention to such spaces, and we’re honing in on a few (both official and unofficial participants) we think are worth visiting. Of course, there are many more events worth your time and attention, from the new Neighbors art fair, a decidedly smaller, invitation-only affair; to the much-beloved Barely Fair, which we wrote about yesterday; to the exhibition smorgasbord happening at 1709 W. Chicago.

At the same time, Berkeley-based Cordy Joan organized the exchange project Transmissions Quilts, in which quiltmaking mirrors the social web of queer artistry: a quilt recipient is nominated; they sit down to record a conversation with a loved one; they choose three trans artists of any medium to translate the conversation into their craft; a quilter incorporates these pieces into a final quilt. “Instructions for Care” brings together these two projects’ dedication to quilts as a site of collective knowledge and queer care networks, strewn across Logan Square’s Gallery Wrightwood. Brown left his unsold paintings, his house, and the two thousand art pieces within it to SAIC upon his death in 1997.
