David Byrne has come to town, and if you haven’t yet been bombarded with giant billboards about it, you may be surprised to discover he’s arrived in an immersive play about the nature of perception called Theater of the Mind. (Disclaimer: Byrne is actually played by eight different actors who rotate the role, and is not physically present.) Seems apt for a guy who has really cashed in on his Warholesque pop image as part of the Talking Heads, transforming it into a life of exploration around art. Not satisfied with five decades of musicianship, he has also written five books, partaken in numerous films and TV shows, and had endless collaborations with artists from many genres.

So a play that explores perceptions about the world through the lens of his youth seems on-brand. Conceived as a traveling show that sticks around each town for a while, Theater of the Mind is currently produced by Goodman Theatre at a site designed specifically for this experience on North LaSalle (coming fresh from its debut in Denver). From the perspective of Chicago theater, it has a broad appeal to audiences of a certain income bracket. It might equally attract theatergoers looking for a more immersive escape-room vibe, Gen Xers who want insight into their musical idol (though his music is mostly absent), and most of all, Chicagoans with visiting family members looking for a way to prove how culturally accessible Chicago art truly is. Kerry Reid and Kimzyn Campbell went the same day and had different David guides. In this review, they enter the theater of their own minds together to explore the themes Byrne has presented.

Theater of the Mind

Through 7/12: first shows as follows (audiences are in groups of 16, admitted every 15 minutes): Tue 5:30 PM, Wed 2 PM, Thu 5:15 PM, Fri 5 PM, Sat noon, Sun 12:30 PM; 333 N. LaSalle, 312-443-3800, goodmantheatre.org or theaterofthemindchicago.com, $69-$99, recommended 10+

To give some background with minimal spoilers: Theater of the Mind, cocreated by Byrne with his wife, writer Mala Gaonkar, takes small groups of people (admitted in 15-minute intervals) through several impressively devised rooms that collectively are meant to represent aspects of memory and perception, illustrating scientific principles along the way (which you can read about in the program afterward—the Davids aren’t delivering lectures during the show). Each audience member is given a nametag at the start renaming them, and your new “character” may be called upon to interact in some low-stress way with your David during the immersive tour.

From a purely technical standpoint, it’s quite a feat, and we would be remiss if we didn’t shout out in particular the stage management and production teams (as well as the front-of-house staff) who keep it all moving smoothly so the various groups never trip over each other on their journey through the mind. Credit of course also to director Andrew Scoville and technology director Heidi Boisvert.

And the “Davids” who serve as our guides represent some of the best that Chicago theater has to offer. You won’t know who your guide is until your experience begins, but with AJ Paramo, James Earl Jones II, Helen Joo Lee, Em Modaff, Shariba Rivers, Elizabeth Laidlaw, Kelli Simpkins, Lucky Stiff, and Victor Musoni all on tap, you will be in good hands.

Theater of whose mind? (Kerry)

Kimzyn, you raised the question in our preliminary discussion of whether David Byrne’s art and life is represented enough or at all in the show. I confess I’m not steeped in his biography. But the fact that he chose to have the guides named “David” and that one of the first things we see is a photo that looks an awful lot like him as a child (with the guides’ clothes, designed by Sarita Fellows, echoing that child’s image) suggests that he does want us to have a more personal connection than just his name stamped on it as a creator. And the references to visiting family in Glasgow certainly make sense, as he was born in Scotland.

But maybe the way he is present the most is that he’s been pretty open about his belief that he’s on the autism spectrum, as in this interview on The Louis Theroux Podcast. (I am not sure that he’s ever had a formal diagnosis.) So much of the show to me feels like it’s about personal perception. What do we pick up on that we’re not specifically told, and is what we’re seeing actually what is in front of us? On the Theroux podcast, Byrne said, “I’ve had the experience where someone will say, ‘Well, I clearly said no,’ and then I’ll replay the conversation and the word ‘no’ was not there, but they expected their facial expression or the nuances of what they were saying to be read and clearly interpreted as a ‘no.’ This isn’t me trying to do something inappropriate. I wasn’t able to read that.”

I also think it’s interesting as a semi-old person myself now to think about how Byrne, at 73, may be thinking of how we construct our memories and our cognitive archives, if you will, to give us something to hold onto about our own lives. Most of us don’t have a body of songs and other creative work as celebrated as his, and I think that by not playing up the musical aspect of his career, the experience is more relatable for general audiences.



But yes, anyone who comes to this thinking they’re going to hear cool interpretations of the Byrne songbook will be disappointed. For that, they can stream American Utopia.

A walk through his brain (Kimzyn)

The part where David Byrne was most invisible to me was, counterintuitively, when we were invited to enter his brain, a huge empty dome full of darkness and echoes and some special effects. There are plenty of optical illusions in the show, and this was the environment that felt most personally interactive with us as the audience, not us playing characters in his life. David asked us to share some personal experiences about a time when reality was less clear to us, all as we waited for total darkness to engulf us. This was probably my favorite moment because it felt the most vulnerable as people stepped up to tell their stories anonymously.

Where do these memories come from? (Kerry)

You and I talked about this at the afterparty and I think it’s absolutely fascinating to think about how memories are formed.

I think that’s what Byrne and Gaonkar are going for. And it’s probably just because I’m far less of a science person than a narrative person that the parts of the show I found most accessible personally were the ones that in some way asked us to examine specific memories. (In my group, I was “Nikko,” who is a friend in David’s young adulthood who had disappointed him in some way, so that was also a bit of a trip as it caused me to think back on people I let down in my early 20s, which was a lot of folks!)

I love that the show uses as bookends the stories of childhood and the attic, which is itself such a powerful metaphor for the place where all the stuff we’re not sure what to do with—but we’re not ready to get rid of—lives in the physical spaces of so many houses. David talking about his mom also felt resonant. Full disclosure: As I write this, I’m coming up on the 18th anniversary of my mom’s death, and I just had a weird-ass dream about her for the first time in a long time this week. But I do think for me at least, as I get older, I think about my parents (and other people I’ve lost) at various stages of their lives and wonder what they thought about toward the end, and what they hoped would remain of themselves after they were gone. So thanks for the memento mori, David. (Also, on another personal note, I was pleasantly surprised that my David was Shariba Rivers, who I had the pleasure of profiling in the Reader’s People issue back in 2023.)

Stowed in the attic (Kimzyn)

The attic stirred up a lot of stuff for us both! When I think about the show as a whole, I think the attic reveal was the crux of it. He is struggling with aligning his childhood memories with his adult understanding of a loved one, regretting the lost opportunities for clarity and closeness. Throughout the show, David mentions how abandoned he felt by his mother as a child. But as an adult in the attic, he musters some empathy and curiosity about her, perhaps even forgives her for being a flawed human, while also recognizing how he was not supported in ways he needed as a child. I think it is really important for many of us to ask ourselves if we are still viewing our early relationships through the lens of a wounded child. Whether or not we can forgive the adults involved is specific to each person, but the power comes from recognizing that we’re not the helpless kid anymore and we can free ourselves from feeling held back by old patterns. For me, the revelation was about giving that little kid inside me some grace for not knowing what they didn’t know. And I really appreciate the curiosity he expressed about what his relationship might have been with his mom. So thanks, David!

The “disco room” in Theater of the Mind Credit: Todd Rosenberg

Disappearing people (Kerry)

As I get older, I have a bit more sympathy for some of the people I’ve lost in my life. But I don’t necessarily feel the need to reconnect with all of them. I don’t plan to have a funeral so I don’t think they’ll be showing up for anything like that, though of course what happens after I’m gone isn’t really in my control. But the central conceit that we are all visitors/mourners/guests at David’s funeral representing various aspects of his life is potentially powerful, though of course it’s also a fun/morbid way to bring us into the various rooms and stories and experiments.

You mentioned the “disappearing people” in the “disco room” as we were talking about this earlier (officially, what we’re experiencing is motion-induced blindness), and that is something I’ve thought about more in the days since the experience than I did right at the time. In the moment, it was just cool. And a little disorienting—I felt a bit like I was on the big centrifuge or Gravitron ride at a carnival, where the walls spin and the floor drops away, though I emphasize it was NOT nausea-inducing as those rides tended to be for me. (If you need to leave at any point in the 75-minute show, you can tell your David and they’ll make sure someone comes to help you out of whatever room you’re in.)

But in retrospect, it was a very cool way of embodying (disembodying?) the people of our youth who are no longer physically in our lives, but whose passions we once felt were our passions, whose secrets were entwined with ours, who we really felt we’d be simpatico with forever. In some cases, we are. In other ways, life did what it does and we moved on. The “motion-induced blindness” is just because our lives moved us out of each other’s eyesight. Now maybe we connect through screens, but not over “miracle berries” at the dance club.

I think there’s a bit of an empathy factor for me now that comes in when I think about people who have ghosted me or who I’ve ghosted. It may not have had anything to do with me (though I have Main Character Syndrome as much as anyone!). It may just be that they were seeing things that weren’t there, or not seeing things they needed, or seeing things they needed that were in a completely different “room” of their lives.

Again, thinking a lot about my mom and my dad and my sister after seeing this show, mostly because I realize how many things I will never know about them. The Chicago poet/performer Lisa Buscani (she was one of the original Neo-Futurists and a 1992 National Poetry Slam champion) wrote a poem about her mom in her 1992 poetry collection Jangle called “Patsy Rocks,” and there’s a line from that which hit me hard in my twenties and even harder now that I don’t have my mom around to ask questions anymore: “And all of her unknown life stands up and demands to be counted.”



I think this show worked emotionally on me more in retrospect than in the moment, perhaps. And maybe that’s a part of how memories work as we reconstruct them, try to make them make sense. (Insert “Stop Making Sense” joke here as necessary!)

Meet me at the disco (Kimzyn)

I think David Byrne’s favorite room might be the disco. It seems to represent the moment in life when we all feel a sense of expansiveness—everything is ahead of us still, we don’t yet have enough life experiences to be weighed down by intergenerational traumas, cyclical waves of historic horrors, etc. We’re just tasting freedom for the first time and all we have is hope, new friends, and novel experiences (them berries again). And yet, as you indicate, there is something so fleeting about the relationships formed in that space. Everyone is just a ship passing in the night that winks out on the horizon. I thought of the many Saturday nights I danced at Reds in South Jersey with my fellow punk pals, thinking we were at the height of our freedom of expression in our podunk town. For some, it might be an LGBTQ+ club, or a sports team that provides that transitional time, but I think it’s a bittersweet universal experience as we enter young adulthood, to think that our youth, friendships, and love will last forever. David Byrne’s Theater of the Mind is an homage, via an introspective peek into the specifics of his past, that resonates with ours, and that communal vibe is what theater is all about.

Community members and legal advocates spoke out Wednesday in Daley Plaza against what they see as brutal arrests and unjust prosecutions stemming from protests outside the ICE facility in Broadview, Illinois. A group of people facing or who have faced criminal charges in Cook County stemming from the protests joined attorneys with the National Lawyers Guild (NLG) of Chicago, and they addressed the more than one hundred people that Illinois police have arrested outside the ICE facility, and the dozens that have faced charges, since September.

Unlike protesters arrested by federal immigration agents during so-called Operation Midway Blitz, who have faced charges in federal court, these people were arrested by Illinois State Police (ISP), Cook County sheriff’s police or local police officers—their cases prosecuted under the office of Cook County state’s attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke.

The Cook County State’s Attorney’s Office said police had directly filed 91 misdemeanors related to activity around the Broadview ICE facility to date. “Of those, we dismissed 63 cases, resolved 8 with pleas, and the remaining cases are pending,” the State’s Attorney’s Office told the Reader in an email. “For felonies, we have declined five cases presented to us that did not meet the charging threshold, and we are currently prosecuting three cases.”

The NLG disputed these figures. Civil rights attorney and NLG member Amanda Yarusso said the group has tracked 102 cases filed in Cook County courthouses from October and November 2025 involving protesters arrested at the Broadview facility.

She said 77 cases have been dismissed and another dismissal is expected this month, five have been resolved by pleas, and NLG attorneys are handling another 17 misdemeanors and two felonies that are still pending. “I know 102 is correct because I am tracking those cases and conferring with the NLG-affiliated volunteer attorneys handling them,” Yarusso said. She added NLG is also tracking 15 new arrests at Broadview since the start of 2026.

Civil rights attorney Amanda Yarusso speaks during a press conference outside the Cook County Circuit Court on April 1, 2026. Credit: Dave Byrnes

The State’s Attorney’s Office responded to the discrepancy by pointing to petty offense citations. “There are some petty tickets that were issued by police—those are not misdemeanors but handled by CCSAO prosecutors,” the office said, adding that 13 such tickets have been dismissed, one is pending and one other has been pleaded out.

Arrests at the Broadview facility, located at 1930 Beach, began in September but ramped up at the start of October. That’s when the ISP and the Cook County Sheriff’s Office, alongside other local police departments, established a “Unified Command” outside the facility. The law enforcement agencies launched the Unified Command to manage protests after federal immigration agents in Broadview fired chemical and less-lethal weapons at protesters, clergy, and press on multiple occasions in September, and amid President Donald Trump’s threats to deploy national guard troops to the Chicago area.

Illinois governor J.B. Pritzker has repeatedly encouraged Illinoisans to peacefully protest the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign. On the eve of Operation Midway Blitz last September, Pritzker asked residents to “be loud for America.” He has defended the creation of the Unified Command, saying it would “prioritize public safety above all else and take steps to safeguard the First Amendment rights of the public.”

However, Nick Milkovich, who was among those arrested during a protest in October, blamed Pritzker and ISP for creating a “chaotic” scene. “I want to be clear that the officers that violently detained me on that day were the Illinois State Police sent by J.B. Pritzker, who said that he was doing so to maintain order,” Milkovich said at Wednesday’s press conference. “Instead what happened is a peaceful protest became chaotic with brutality.”

Another person arrested at a Broadview protest who spoke Wednesday, who only gave her name as Miriam, urged people to keep the focus off protesters and on the immigrant community members that ICE continues to abduct. But NLG attorney Mariah Garcia said Miriam and others had downplayed the violence of their own arrests. “People were hit with billy clubs. Pritzker’s office did not respond to a request for comment regarding Illinoisans who have faced physical violence and arrest over peaceful protest activities.

State and local police with Unified Command have effectively served as a guard contingent for the Broadview ICE jail, despite the TRUST Act, an Illinois law that largely bars local law enforcement from coordinating with federal immigration authorities.

When Illinois and the City of Chicago were fighting President Donald Trump in federal court last fall over his attempt to deploy national guard troops to the area, the state and city even cited the Unified Command’s actions to support their argument that such a deployment would be unwarranted. “Multiple state and local law enforcement agencies, including the Illinois State Police, have formed a unified command in Broadview to manage public safety and protect First Amendment rights around ICE’s facility,” the city and state said in an October 6 federal court filing.

Yarusso and the NLG argued this violates the TRUST Act, which states, “unless presented with a federal criminal warrant, or otherwise required by federal law,” law enforcement agencies and officials are not allowed to support federal immigration agents’ operations, including by “establishing a security or traffic perimeter surrounding such operations.”

Illinois attorney general Kwame Raoul, whose office is tasked with investigating violations of the TRUST Act, has previously maintained in statements to the Reader that such actions do not run afoul of the law.

A spokesperson for the Cook County Sheriff’s Office likewise denied its officers’ conduct in Broadview violated the TRUST Act, arguing they have instead acted to defuse conflict between protesters and federal agents.

“Prior to the formation of the Temporary Unified Command on October 2, escalating violence between protestors and federal agents outside the Broadview facility posed a significant public safety threat and severely degraded the quality of life for residents and business owners in the surrounding area,” the sheriff’s office told the Reader. “The command was established to address these problems, and since then thousands upon thousands of individuals—including National Lawyers Guild members—have been able to safely and lawfully exercise their First Amendment Right to protest outside the facility.”

Since October, protesters have had to contend with shifting regulations from both the Unified Command and the Village of Broadview that have sought to restrict when and where protest is allowed. In early October, the Unified Command designated two “protest areas” along Beach Street’s sidewalks, a block north of the jail. Broadview mayor Katrina Thompson signed an executive order on October 6 which only allowed demonstrations between the hours of 9 AM and 6 PM; her subsequent October 12 executive order closed the sidewalks along a two-block stretch of 25th Avenue, a busy street adjacent to the ICE facility which had also seen protests. Police arrested or threatened to arrest those who overstepped the occasionally overcrowded protest areas into the street or who resisted the 6 PM curfew.

The Unified Command expanded the designated protest area to include a larger section of Beach Street on November 18. Four days earlier, at a large protest organized by faith leaders, multiple media outlets, including the Reader, captured an ISP officer grabbing Reverend Michael Woolf of the Lake Street Church of Evanston by the arm and tackling him to the ground with the assistance of multiple other officers. The officer grabbed Woolf without any provocation, save that he was in the street at the front of a larger crowd.

Thompson added new dimensions to her curfew in a December 3 executive order, allowing protesters to stay out from 9 AM to 9 PM or 11 AM to 7 PM depending on whether there were fewer or more than 25 protesters present, respectively.

On March 22, U.S. district judge Edmond Chang blocked the village from enforcing those time restrictions, finding they “cannot stand under the First Amendment.” Chang did not bar the village from “enacting more specific limits for specific protests on specific days.”

In one pending Cook County misdemeanor case the Reader reviewed, attorneys associated with the NLG moved for the case to be dismissed on grounds of First Amendment and due process violations, citing Chang’s order.

The NLG is skeptical of the other Cook County cases which remain pending, saying in a press statement that “in many of these pending cases, based on attorneys’ review of the body worn camera footage tendered in discovery, the arrests and charges are not supported by the evidence.”

State’s attorney O’Neill Burke, meanwhile, has denied her office has the authority to lead investigations into potential misconduct by federal immigration agents, even as multiple Illinois lawmakers and civil rights advocates have signed a petition calling for the Circuit Court of Cook County to appoint a special prosecutor to conduct such investigations in her place.

Dr. Charles Joseph Smith wants to stage an opera called War of the Martian Ghosts. In 2018, he issued an album of neoclassical piano pieces with that title through local indie Sooper Records. On April 3, the label will release a compilation of Smith’s recordings that spans a 30-year period called Collected Works and War of the Martian Ghosts.

I’ve come to the Smith family home in Beverly to discuss the new collection, but Smith steers the conversation where he wants. For the most part, I let him. This is how I learn that he developed the Martian Ghosts concept in 1996, while earning a doctorate of musical arts at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.

The idea arrived, he explains, while he worked on a Kurzweil PC88 keyboard. He found a patch that produced laserlike sounds, then recorded an improvisation with a Master Tracks Pro software sequencer. “I titled it ‘War of the Martian Ghosts’ because it sounds like a war for about four and a half minutes,” he says.

Smith’s 2018 Sooper release, his debut for the label, aroused his interest in making War of the Martian Ghosts into an actual opera. “I realized over the years I’ve been exposed to musicals that have been turned into operas,” he says. “I’ve seen the success of The Phantom of the Opera. I didn’t see The Who’s Tommy, but I did see Jesus Christ Superstar. So if they can do operas, why not me?”

The piano music he recorded for War of the Martian Ghosts was part of an ongoing process of revision and expansion. He’s since added lyrics and written arias for an orchestral arrangement with vocal soloists. He says the version he completed in 2022 runs two hours, maybe two and a half.

“I was gonna try to produce it, but now it’s still a bit way off,” Smith says. “I realized if I wanted to do that, it’s gonna cost me a lot of money—twenty thousand dollars. I was trying to look for grants, maybe even tell Chicago Opera Theater to do that—they do contemporary avant-garde operas. I was afraid they’d say no. I’m still a bit shy about doing this.” The 32 tracks on Charles Joseph Smith’s new archival collection span three decades. If you’ve seen Smith at a show, you might be surprised to hear him describe himself as shy. For more than two decades, he’s been frequenting DIY venues, artsy underground rock shows, and avant-garde concerts, as a fan and sometimes as a performer. You’ll often spot him dancing right up by the stage. And when he dances, it’s impossible to mistake him for anyone else.

Smith is a short, wiry Black man, and he wears thick eyeglasses held on with an even thicker retainer strap—which must help when he’s caught up in the music. Smith is autistic, and he moves with joyful abandon and what looks like a total lack of self-consciousness. He dances with his entire body, and it’s easy to imagine his glasses flying off during a sudden lunge or pivot. A Retrospective on Musician Charles Joseph Smith
